families.name: Traditional & Mainstream
families.blurb: The acoustic through-line: New Orleans to swing to bebop to hard bop to the modern mainstream.

families.name: Avant-Garde & Composed
families.blurb: The experimental and composed wing — free jazz, the collectives, European improvisation, chamber jazz.

families.name: Electric & Crossover
families.blurb: Amplified, groove-first and producer-shaped: fusion, funk, and everything downstream of the sampler.

families.name: Global Currents
families.blurb: Jazz built on rhythmic systems from outside the United States, and the scenes that grew around them.

genres.name: Ragtime

origin.city: Sedalia / St. Louis / Missouri river towns

genres.oneLine: Written-out piano music where the left hand marches and the right hand refuses to land on the beat.
genres.summary: Put your foot on the floor with the left hand — steady, even, oom-pah, like a march. Now listen to what the right hand does over the top: it keeps arriving a half-beat early, tugging against that floor. That tug is the whole idea, and 'ragged time' is where the name comes from. Ragtime is composed music, published as sheet music and sold by the ton between 1899 and 1917, mostly in multi-strain march form: four separate 16-bar tunes played in sequence, each repeated, often with a key change for the third. It is not improvised, which is why some writers refuse to call it jazz at all. But every early jazz pianist learned it, the New Orleans repertoire was built out of it, and the syncopation habit it drilled into American ears is the precondition for everything downstream. Scott Joplin wanted it treated as concert music and wrote an opera to prove the point; the market wanted novelty numbers and cakewalks. Both things happened.

musicalTraits.harmony: Straightforward European parlour harmony — tonic, dominant, secondary dominants, brisk circle-of-fifths runs. Blues notes are rare; this is not blues-derived music.
musicalTraits.rhythm: An unvarying duple left hand under a right hand full of tied-over, off-beat accents. The syncopation is written, not felt in the moment.
musicalTraits.form: Multi-strain march form: AABBACCDD or similar, 16 bars per strain, with the C strain ('the trio') usually in the subdominant.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Solo piano first and foremost; also banjo, brass band, and the ragtime orchestras that played from stock arrangements.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Essentially none in the classic repertoire. Performers were expected to play the printed notes, and Joplin famously instructed that it never be played fast.
musicalTraits.timbre: Bright upright piano, often slightly out of tune, in a room with hard surfaces. Cleanness and evenness of touch were the prized virtues.

earMarkers: A steady oom-pah left hand that never varies while the melody keeps landing between the beats
Four distinctly different tunes inside one piece, each played twice before moving on
A key change roughly halfway through, usually up a fourth, when the 'trio' section arrives
No drums, no bass, no horns — one piano doing all of it

keyFigures.name: Scott Joplin
keyFigures.why: Wrote the rags that defined the classic style and fought to have it heard as art music rather than novelty.

keyFigures.name: James Scott
keyFigures.why: The most rhythmically intricate of the classic ragtime composers; his right-hand writing is harder than Joplin's.

keyFigures.name: Joseph Lamb
keyFigures.why: The third of the 'big three' and the only white composer among them; wrote the style's most harmonically ambitious pieces.

keyFigures.name: Jelly Roll Morton
keyFigures.why: The hinge figure — took rag form and loosened it with swing, blues and what he called the 'Spanish tinge'.

genres.contested: Whether ragtime is jazz at all. It has no improvisation and no blues content, and Gunther Schuller and others treat it strictly as a precursor. Ragtime scholars often resent its absorption into jazz history entirely. This guide treats it as a root rather than a branch.

genres.name: New Orleans Jazz
genres.oneLine: Three horns improvising different melodies at the same time over a marching-band rhythm section, and somehow it works.
genres.summary: The sound is a polite pile-up. Cornet states the tune in the middle register, clarinet weaves a busy countermelody above it, trombone slides around underneath filling the gaps — all three at once, all the time, nobody waiting their turn. This collective improvisation is the defining feature and the thing that disappeared from jazz almost immediately afterward. Underneath, banjo and tuba or bass mark the beat with the rhythm section still audibly descended from brass bands and street parades. The repertoire came from marches, rags, hymns, blues, and popular songs, and the ensemble had a fixed division of labour that everyone understood, which is what kept the counterpoint from becoming noise. It was recorded first in 1917 by a white band, the Original Dixieland Jass Band, which is a fact worth sitting with: the music was Black in origin and the record industry got there in the wrong order. King Oliver's 1923 sessions and Armstrong's Hot Fives are where you actually hear what the style could do.

musicalTraits.harmony: Simple and functional — I, IV, V with passing diminished chords. Blues form sits alongside 32-bar song and multi-strain rag form.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Two-beat, with the accent on 1 and 3 and a distinct march inheritance. The 'stomp' feel is heavier and squarer than later swing.
musicalTraits.form: Head arrangements over the tune's chorus structure, with breaks, stop-time passages, and a final out-chorus where everyone plays louder.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Front line of cornet/trumpet, clarinet, trombone; rhythm section of banjo or guitar, tuba or string bass, drums, sometimes piano.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Collective and simultaneous rather than one soloist at a time. Individual paraphrase of the melody rather than running the changes.
musicalTraits.timbre: Vibrato-heavy, vocalised brass — growls, smears, plunger mutes. Nobody is trying to sound clean.

earMarkers: Three horns playing three different melodies at once, and you can pick out each one
The clarinet noodling high and fast above everything else
Trombone smearing between notes rather than hitting them squarely
A two-beat oom-pah bass line, not the even four of later jazz
Everyone getting louder and busier for the last chorus

keyFigures.name: Louis Armstrong
keyFigures.why: Turned the ensemble style inside out by proving a single soloist could carry a record; the pivot from collective to individual runs through him.

keyFigures.name: King Oliver
keyFigures.why: Led the Creole Jazz Band, the best-documented example of the two-cornet New Orleans ensemble working properly.

keyFigures.name: Sidney Bechet
keyFigures.why: The first great jazz soloist on record alongside Armstrong; his wide vibrato is the sound of the idiom's clarinet lineage.

keyFigures.name: Jelly Roll Morton
keyFigures.why: Arranged the style rather than just playing it — his Red Hot Peppers sides are composed frameworks with improvisation slotted in.

genres.contested: 'Dixieland' and 'New Orleans jazz' are often used interchangeably, but many musicians and writers use 'Dixieland' specifically for the later white revivalist style and consider the term loaded. There is also a live argument about whether the 1940s revival was preservation or pastiche.

genres.name: Chicago Jazz
genres.oneLine: New Orleans jazz after the Great Migration, played hotter and faster by kids who learned it off records.
genres.summary: When the New Orleans players moved north during the Great Migration, a generation of young white Chicagoans — the Austin High Gang among them — learned the music by wearing out King Oliver records and then playing it their own way. What came out was tenser than the original. The collective front line is still there but thinner, the tempos are up, the saxophone starts elbowing into the front line where it never belonged in New Orleans, and there is a nervous, driving quality to the rhythm that the older players did not have. The signature device is the 'explosion' — a hard accented break, often on the last beat before a chorus. It is transitional music: still ensemble-based, but with individual solos taking up more and more space until, by about 1930, the format simply became the small swing band. Its historical importance is partly demographic — this is where jazz stopped being regional and became a national commercial music.

musicalTraits.harmony: Same functional harmony as New Orleans, with more use of the 32-bar popular song form and slightly richer passing chords.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Faster and more forward-leaning than New Orleans, with a shift away from two-beat towards an even four. Tense rather than rolling.
musicalTraits.form: Head–solos–head. The out-chorus survives, but the sequence of individual solos is now the centre of the record.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Cornet, clarinet, trombone, plus tenor or C-melody saxophone; guitar replacing banjo, string bass replacing tuba.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Individual solo choruses become the point. Bix Beiderbecke's cool, placed lyricism and Frank Teschemacher's jagged clarinet are the two poles.
musicalTraits.timbre: Brighter and drier than New Orleans; Beiderbecke's bell-like cornet tone is deliberately un-vibrato'd and became a model for cool jazz twenty years later.

earMarkers: Faster tempos and a jumpier, more anxious feel than New Orleans records
A hard accented 'explosion' hit just before a new chorus starts
A saxophone in the front line, which New Orleans bands mostly did not have
Long individual solos rather than continuous group weaving

keyFigures.name: Bix Beiderbecke
keyFigures.why: Played with a round, unforced tone and unusual interval choices; the first widely copied alternative to Armstrong's approach.

keyFigures.name: Eddie Condon
keyFigures.why: Organiser and lifelong advocate; his sessions kept the style documented for four decades.

keyFigures.name: Frank Teschemacher
keyFigures.why: The jagged, harmonically restless clarinet voice of the style, killed in a car crash at 26.

keyFigures.name: Gene Krupa
keyFigures.why: Brought the full drum kit forward in the mix and carried the Chicago drive into the swing era.

genres.contested: Whether 'Chicago style' names a genuine musical style or just a place and a cohort. Some writers treat it as a white derivative of New Orleans jazz rather than a development; others point to the rhythmic shift toward four-beat as a real innovation that fed the swing era.

genres.name: Stride Piano
genres.oneLine: Ragtime's left hand taught to swing, played by men competing to physically overwhelm each other at rent parties.
genres.summary: The left hand leaps: bass note on 1 and 3, chord up in the middle of the keyboard on 2 and 4, back and forth across a tenth or more. That leap is the stride, and it is genuinely hard — the reach alone excluded a lot of players. Where ragtime's left hand was even and metronomic, stride's is springy and slightly ahead or behind, and the right hand is no longer bound to the printed page. This was competitive music. Harlem rent parties in the 1920s ran on cutting contests, where pianists took turns trying to demolish each other, and the style's showmanship — the tempo escalations, the interpolated classical quotations, the sheer density — comes directly from that. James P. Johnson is the founding figure, Willie 'The Lion' Smith the great character, and Fats Waller the one who took it to a mass audience by adding comedy and a hit-making instinct. Art Tatum then took the technique somewhere nobody has followed since. Ellington, Basie and Monk all played stride, and you can hear it surfacing in their playing decades later.

musicalTraits.harmony: Richer than ragtime — sixths, ninths, chromatic passing chords, and a growing use of blues inflection. Tatum pushed it into substitutions that anticipated bebop.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Alternating bass-note/chord left hand at speed, with rhythmic elasticity the right hand plays against. Swing eighth notes replace ragtime's even ones.
musicalTraits.form: Popular song forms and rag strains, with the arrangement built as a series of escalating choruses.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Solo piano. The whole point is that one player covers bass, chords, and melody without help.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Extensive right-hand variation over a memorised structure, plus reharmonisation and interpolated quotation.
musicalTraits.timbre: Full-range, orchestral use of the piano — deep bass, ringing treble, heavy pedalling on ballads.

earMarkers: The left hand physically jumping between a low bass note and a mid-range chord, over and over
One pianist producing a whole band's worth of sound with no rhythm section
Tempos that ratchet up as the performance goes on, showing off
Sudden quotations from classical pieces or other songs dropped in mid-solo

keyFigures.name: James P. Johnson
keyFigures.why: The founder; 'Carolina Shout' was the test piece every aspiring Harlem pianist had to master.

keyFigures.name: Fats Waller
keyFigures.why: Johnson's student, and the one who made the style commercially enormous without diluting the left hand.

keyFigures.name: Willie 'The Lion' Smith
keyFigures.why: The most harmonically impressionistic of the strider; Ellington cited him directly as an influence.

keyFigures.name: Art Tatum
keyFigures.why: Took stride's mechanics and applied a harmonic imagination and technique that reset what the instrument could do.

genres.contested: Whether Art Tatum belongs inside stride or outside it. His left hand is stride-derived, but his harmonic language points forward to bebop; some historians file him as a category of one.

genres.name: Kansas City Jazz
genres.oneLine: Blues-soaked big band jazz built on riffs, with a rhythm section so relaxed it seems to float.
genres.summary: Kansas City under the Pendergast machine had wide-open nightlife and clubs that stayed open all night, which meant jam sessions ran for hours and a musician's reputation was made in them. Two things came out of that. First, riff-based arranging: instead of writing intricate charts, sections trade short repeated phrases, building layer on layer, and the arrangement can be assembled on the bandstand by ear. Second, a new rhythm section feel — Basie's band with Walter Page on bass, Freddie Green on guitar and Jo Jones on drums shifted the pulse to an even, buoyant four beats to the bar, moved timekeeping to the hi-hat and ride, and left enormous space. Basie's own piano playing reduced to a few notes, which was a radical act of subtraction. Blues form is everywhere, far more than in eastern swing bands. And the marathon jam sessions turned tenor saxophone into a combat sport, which produced Lester Young — whose light, behind-the-beat lyricism became the direct model for Charlie Parker's generation.

musicalTraits.harmony: Blues-dominant. Twelve-bar form is the default rather than an occasional feature, with simple changes that leave room for the soloist.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Even four-to-the-bar with a light, springing feel. Bass walks, guitar chunks quarter notes, drums move time to the hi-hat and use the bass drum sparingly.
musicalTraits.form: Head arrangements built from riffs, with call-and-response between brass and reeds, and long strings of solo choruses.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Full big band, but also the small jam-session combo. Guitar is a rhythm instrument, not a solo voice.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Chorus after chorus over the blues, with the expectation that a soloist builds across many choruses rather than saying it all in one.
musicalTraits.timbre: Lester Young's dry, vibratoless tenor against Coleman Hawkins' heavier eastern sound — the two poles of saxophone tone for the next twenty years.

earMarkers: Short repeated phrases stacked in layers, brass answering reeds
Twelve-bar blues far more often than in other big band music
A rhythm section that feels like it's gliding rather than pushing
Piano that plays almost nothing — a few notes, then silence
Solos that go on for four, six, eight choruses and keep building

keyFigures.name: Count Basie
keyFigures.why: Built the rhythm section that redefined swing feel, and made minimalism at the piano a style rather than an absence.

keyFigures.name: Lester Young
keyFigures.why: Played light, behind the beat, with long asymmetric lines — the direct precursor to bebop phrasing and to cool jazz tone.

keyFigures.name: Bennie Moten
keyFigures.why: Led the band that became Basie's; the 1932 Victor sessions are where the KC rhythmic shift first lands on record.

keyFigures.name: Mary Lou Williams
keyFigures.why: Chief arranger for Andy Kirk's Clouds of Joy and the KC scene's most important compositional mind; later mentored the bebop generation.

keyFigures.name: Jay McShann
keyFigures.why: Ran the band where Charlie Parker got his first recorded solos, making the KC-to-bebop link literal.

genres.contested: Whether Kansas City is a separate genre or a regional dialect of swing. This guide treats it separately because the rhythmic and blues-form innovations there are specific, traceable, and fed bebop more directly than the New York swing mainstream did.

genres.name: Swing & Big Band
genres.oneLine: Jazz as America's pop music: written arrangements for fourteen-plus players, built for dancing.
genres.summary: For about a decade, this was simply what popular music sounded like. The instrument is the orchestra: reeds and brass as blocks of sound answering each other, a rhythm section keeping an even four, and arrangements written down so a large band could execute complicated material precisely night after night. The arranger becomes as important as any soloist — Fletcher Henderson, Sy Oliver, Eddie Sauter, Billy Strayhorn. What separates swing from the dance music before it is the rhythmic feel: uneven eighth notes with a forward lean, and a rhythm section that propels rather than merely marks time. Within that commercial frame there was enormous range, from Glenn Miller's tightly controlled hits through Benny Goodman's virtuoso precision to Ellington's orchestra, which was really a composer's laboratory with an unusually stable roster. Its commercial dominance ended after 1946 — economics, a wartime recording ban, changing dance habits, the entertainment tax — but big band writing never stopped, and the repertory and contemporary large-ensemble scenes are direct continuations.

musicalTraits.harmony: Popular song harmony of the era, richly voiced — added sixths and ninths, sectional block voicings, and increasingly adventurous writing as the 1940s approach.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Even four-to-the-bar with swung eighths. The rhythm section is a unit whose job is lift.
musicalTraits.form: Written arrangements on 32-bar AABA popular songs and blues, with solos slotted into designated choruses and shout choruses near the end.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Standardised big band: four or five reeds, three or four trumpets, three or four trombones, piano, guitar, bass, drums. Often a featured vocalist.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Present but rationed — usually one or two choruses inside an otherwise written chart.
musicalTraits.timbre: Section blend as the primary colour: saxophones as a single voice, brass with and without mutes, and the deliberate contrast between the two.

earMarkers: Whole sections of horns moving together in harmony, like one huge instrument
Brass and reeds trading phrases back and forth in call-and-response
A hard-hitting climactic 'shout chorus' near the end where the whole band goes up a gear
Danceable, steady tempos — this was functional music for a ballroom floor

keyFigures.name: Duke Ellington
keyFigures.why: Wrote for the specific players in his band rather than for generic parts, which is why his music does not transfer well to other orchestras.

keyFigures.name: Fletcher Henderson
keyFigures.why: Codified the reed-versus-brass call-and-response template that the entire era used, then sold his charts to Goodman.

keyFigures.name: Benny Goodman
keyFigures.why: Made swing a mass phenomenon in 1935 and led racially integrated small groups in public when that was a professional risk.

keyFigures.name: Billy Strayhorn
keyFigures.why: Ellington's writing partner for nearly thirty years; the harmonic sophistication of the later Ellington book is substantially his.

keyFigures.name: Coleman Hawkins
keyFigures.why: His 1939 'Body and Soul' is a full chorus of improvisation on the harmony rather than the melody — a bebop premise, two years early.

genres.contested: Where swing ends. Some treat 1946 as the hard stop; others point to Basie's second band, Kenton, Herman's Herds and the entire repertory movement as evidence that it simply stopped being pop music without ceasing to exist. This guide takes the latter view.

genres.name: Jazz Manouche
genres.oneLine: Swing played on acoustic guitars with no drums, where the rhythm guitars are the drum kit.
genres.summary: No drums, no horns, no piano — two or three acoustic guitars, a violin, and a double bass. The rhythm guitars play 'la pompe', a percussive chunk-chunk on every beat with the chord damped immediately, and that sound does the entire job of a drum kit. Over it, a lead guitar plays fast, ornamented single-note lines full of arpeggios, chromatic runs, and a wide fingered vibrato that comes out of Romani string tradition rather than American jazz. Django Reinhardt built the style with violinist Stéphane Grappelli in the Quintette du Hot Club de France, formed in Paris in 1934, and he did it with two working fingers on his fretting hand after a caravan fire — the resulting chord voicings and octave-heavy lines are partly a workaround that became a vocabulary. The repertoire mixes American standards with French musette waltzes and Django's own compositions. It is one of the very few jazz styles born outside the United States that fed back into the American mainstream, and it remains a living tradition with festivals, dynasties and a defined technique.

musicalTraits.harmony: Swing-era changes with a strong minor-key and diminished flavour, plus musette-derived chromaticism. Sixth and diminished chords everywhere.
musicalTraits.rhythm: 'La pompe' — a damped, percussive four-to-the-bar guitar stroke with a hard accent on 2 and 4 that replaces drums entirely.
musicalTraits.form: Standards and originals in 32-bar and 16-bar forms, often taken at extreme tempos, with breaks and unaccompanied intros.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Lead guitar, one or two rhythm guitars, violin, double bass. Selmer-Maccaferri guitars with a distinctive cutting tone.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Fast arpeggio-based lines, chromatic approach notes, tremolo and octave passages. More ornamental and less blues-inflected than American jazz of the same era.
musicalTraits.timbre: All-acoustic, bright and nasal. Wide, fast vibrato on both guitar and violin.

earMarkers: Guitars chopping out every beat with the chord cut short — that's the drum kit
Absolutely no drums and no horns anywhere
Lead guitar lines running up and down arpeggios at improbable speed
Violin as a front-line solo instrument, which is rare elsewhere in jazz
A wide, fast shimmer of vibrato at the end of held notes

keyFigures.name: Django Reinhardt
keyFigures.why: Invented the idiom's guitar language, with a fretting hand damaged by fire that forced a distinctive approach to voicings and octaves.

keyFigures.name: Stéphane Grappelli
keyFigures.why: Made violin a credible jazz lead voice and carried the style forward for fifty years after Django's death.

keyFigures.name: Biréli Lagrène
keyFigures.why: The most prominent of the modern inheritors; recorded as a teenage prodigy and later moved between manouche and fusion.

keyFigures.name: Baro Ferret
keyFigures.why: Key figure in the Parisian Romani guitar scene whose musette-inflected playing shows the style's non-American roots.

genres.contested: The name. 'Gypsy jazz' is standard in English-language usage but 'Gypsy' is widely considered a slur by Romani people; 'jazz manouche' is the French term and is preferred by many players. This guide leads with the latter. There is also debate over whether Django's postwar electric bebop-influenced work is the same genre at all.

genres.name: Vocal Jazz & the Songbook
genres.oneLine: Singers treating a written song as raw material — bending the time, the pitch and the meaning of the lyric.
genres.summary: The difference between a jazz singer and a good singer of the same songs is what they do to the tune. Billie Holiday takes a mediocre Tin Pan Alley number, strips the melody down to a few notes, drags every phrase behind the beat, and makes the lyric mean something the writer never intended. Ella Fitzgerald keeps the melody gleaming and then improvises whole choruses of wordless scat with the accuracy of a horn player. Sarah Vaughan uses an operatically trained instrument to reharmonise on the fly. All three are doing the same underlying thing — improvising, in the specific sense that they are making choices about time and pitch that are not in the sheet music. The repertoire is largely the Great American Songbook: Gershwin, Porter, Berlin, Kern, Rodgers, Arlen, written mostly for Broadway and Hollywood between the 1920s and 1950s, whose 32-bar AABA forms became the harmonic playing field for jazz instrumentalists too. Scat singing is the most obvious marker but far from the most important one; phrasing is.

musicalTraits.harmony: Songbook harmony — 32-bar AABA and ABAC forms with rich ii–V movement. Singers often introduce their own passing notes and blue thirds against it.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Radical flexibility with the beat. Holiday sits far behind it, Sinatra stretches phrases across bar lines, Fitzgerald floats on top of it.
musicalTraits.form: Verse (often omitted) then chorus, with instrumental solo sections and a final chorus that departs furthest from the written melody.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Voice with anything from solo piano to full string orchestra; the small-group-with-horns setting is where the interplay is most audible.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Melodic paraphrase first, scat second. The best singers vary the melody so continuously that the written line never returns intact.
musicalTraits.timbre: Enormous range, from Holiday's small, frayed sound to Vaughan's four-octave control. Vibrato use is a stylistic signature in itself.

earMarkers: The singer arriving noticeably late on words, letting the band go ahead
The written melody getting further from itself with each chorus
Wordless syllables used as an instrumental solo (scat)
Conversational give-and-take between the voice and one instrument — Holiday and Lester Young are the model

keyFigures.name: Billie Holiday
keyFigures.why: Rewrote what phrasing could do; her interpretive approach to a lyric is the reference point for everyone who followed.

keyFigures.name: Ella Fitzgerald
keyFigures.why: The most technically complete scat improviser, and her Songbook series fixed the canon of American popular song.

keyFigures.name: Sarah Vaughan
keyFigures.why: Brought bebop harmony and operatic technique to the same phrase; the most harmonically daring of the major singers.

keyFigures.name: Louis Armstrong
keyFigures.why: Established that a jazz singer phrases like a horn player, and popularised scat in the 1920s.

keyFigures.name: Betty Carter
keyFigures.why: Took the abstraction furthest — extreme tempos, melodies dismantled beyond recognition, and a band she ran like a bebop leader.

genres.contested: Whether 'vocal jazz' is a genre or a role that cuts across every genre. Purists argue that Sinatra and much of the Songbook repertoire is popular singing with jazz accompaniment rather than jazz. This guide treats it as a genre-shaped tradition with a defined repertoire and a distinct set of techniques, while acknowledging the boundary is porous — an interpretive call, not a settled fact.

genres.name: Bebop
genres.oneLine: Small-group jazz played fast and dense enough that it stopped being dance music and became something you sit down for.
genres.summary: Bebop is what happens when musicians decide the audience is other musicians. A small group — trumpet, alto or tenor, piano, bass, drums — plays a fast, angular unison melody, then everyone solos at length over the chord changes, then the melody returns. The tunes are often new heads written over the harmony of existing standards, so the players get fresh material without paying royalties or relearning forms. The lines are long, asymmetric, and full of chromatic approach notes and upper-structure intervals — flattened fifths and ninths that sounded wrong to swing-trained ears. Rhythmically the whole timekeeping apparatus moves: the ride cymbal carries the pulse, the bass drum stops marking every beat and instead 'drops bombs' as accents, and the pianist stops stride-style timekeeping and comps in irregular stabs. It developed at after-hours sessions in Harlem, notably Minton's Playhouse, during the early 1940s, and the 1942–44 recording ban means the crucial transition is largely undocumented — the records pick up when the style is already formed.

musicalTraits.harmony: Fast-moving functional harmony with extensions and substitutions: flat nines, sharp elevens, tritone substitutions, and ii–V chains inserted where the original song had none.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Ride cymbal as primary timekeeper, walking bass in even four, bass drum used for irregular accents rather than pulse, piano comping in syncopated punctuation.
musicalTraits.form: Head–solos–head over 32-bar AABA, rhythm changes, and 12-bar blues. Contrafacts — new melodies on borrowed changes — are everywhere.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Quintet: trumpet, saxophone, piano, bass, drums. Guitar drops out of the rhythm section.
musicalTraits.improvisation: The central activity. Long eighth-note lines that outline the harmony precisely, with chromatic enclosures and deliberate targeting of the upper extensions.
musicalTraits.timbre: Dry, hard, minimal vibrato. Parker's alto tone and Gillespie's high, brilliant trumpet are deliberately unsentimental.

earMarkers: A fast, twisting melody played in unison by two horns with no harmony underneath
Drums keeping time on a cymbal while the bass drum punches at unpredictable moments
Solos that run in continuous eighth notes for a very long time without obvious pause
Tunes you half-recognise — the chords are from a standard but the melody is new
Tempos that are simply too fast to dance to

keyFigures.name: Charlie Parker
keyFigures.why: Built the melodic vocabulary. Almost every jazz improviser since has absorbed his phrasing, whether or not they play his style.

keyFigures.name: Dizzy Gillespie
keyFigures.why: Parker's counterpart and the style's theorist and teacher; also the one who brought Afro-Cuban rhythm into it.

keyFigures.name: Bud Powell
keyFigures.why: Translated Parker's horn lines to the keyboard and invented the modern jazz piano role — right-hand lines over sparse left-hand chords.

keyFigures.name: Thelonious Monk
keyFigures.why: Present at the creation but never really a bebop player; his compositions and use of space run at an angle to the whole style.

keyFigures.name: Max Roach
keyFigures.why: Moved the drum kit from timekeeping to conversation, playing melodically against the soloist.

keyFigures.name: Kenny Clarke
keyFigures.why: The Minton's house drummer who first shifted the pulse to the ride cymbal — the technical change that made bebop possible.

genres.contested: Whether bebop was a revolution or an evolution. Musicians involved often described it as a natural extension of what Lester Young, Charlie Christian and Coleman Hawkins were already doing; the press framed it as a rupture. Both accounts have evidence behind them.

genres.name: Cool Jazz
genres.oneLine: Bebop's harmony at half the temperature — soft attack, written counterpoint, and space where the heat used to be.
genres.summary: Take bebop's harmonic sophistication and remove its aggression. Cool jazz keeps the extended chords and the fast changes but plays them with a light, vibrato-free tone, at moderate tempos, with far more written material and much more silence. The Miles Davis nonet sessions of 1949–50 are the founding document: nine pieces including French horn and tuba, arranged by Gil Evans, Gerry Mulligan and John Lewis into something closer to chamber music than to a jam session. The other root is Lennie Tristano's circle in New York, which pursued long, seamless improvised lines with almost no rhythmic emphasis, deliberately suppressing the drama. Lester Young is the shared ancestor of both — his dry tone and behind-the-beat placement is what 'cool' means as a sound. Critics have often written the style off as bloodless or as a whitening of bebop, and the racial politics of its reception are genuinely ugly, but the actual music of Tristano, Konitz, Evans and Lewis is intellectually demanding and unlike anything else.

musicalTraits.harmony: Bebop's extended harmony plus impressionist colouring — quartal voicings, whole-tone passages, and polytonal writing in the arranged pieces.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Even, unemphatic, deliberately undramatic. Drummers use brushes often and avoid punctuation; the pulse is stated rather than driven.
musicalTraits.form: Arranged ensemble passages framing solos, with contrapuntal writing and unusual section lengths rather than straight head–solos–head.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Unusual for jazz: French horn, tuba, baritone saxophone, flute, cello. Piano-less groups also appear.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Long, evenly phrased melodic lines with little rhythmic display. Tristano's students practised eliminating cliché and accent entirely.
musicalTraits.timbre: Soft attack, minimal vibrato, blended ensemble sound. Nothing is played loudly for effect.

earMarkers: Horns playing with a soft, breathy tone and almost no vibrato
Two or more melody lines moving independently in a written arrangement, not just chords
Instruments you don't expect in jazz — French horn, tuba, cello
Drums using brushes and staying out of the way
Medium tempos with noticeable space between phrases

keyFigures.name: Miles Davis
keyFigures.why: Assembled the nonet and provided its middle-register, unhurried lead voice; then left the style behind within a few years.

keyFigures.name: Gil Evans
keyFigures.why: The orchestral imagination behind the nonet and later the Davis–Evans collaborations; treated the ensemble as a single instrument with variable colour.

keyFigures.name: Lennie Tristano
keyFigures.why: Ran a rigorous school of improvisation aimed at pure line, and cut two free improvisations in 1949, years before Ornette Coleman.

keyFigures.name: Lee Konitz
keyFigures.why: The one major altoist of his generation who did not sound like Charlie Parker — a genuine alternative line of descent.

keyFigures.name: John Lewis
keyFigures.why: Nonet arranger who then built the Modern Jazz Quartet around baroque counterpoint and blues.

genres.contested: Whether cool jazz and West Coast jazz are one thing. This guide separates them: cool jazz is the New York nonet/Tristano lineage, West Coast is the Los Angeles studio-musician scene that grew partly out of it. Many writers merge the two, and the overlap in personnel is real.

genres.name: West Coast Jazz
genres.oneLine: Cool jazz relocated to LA studios: light, arranged, lyrical, and made by musicians with day jobs scoring films.
genres.summary: Los Angeles in the 1950s had a large population of superb reading musicians working in film and television studios, and a club scene — the Lighthouse in Hermosa Beach, Zardi's, the Haig — where they played jazz at night. The result is a music that prizes arrangement, clarity and craft: contrapuntal writing, unusual instrumentation, tightly rehearsed ensembles, and solos that stay lyrical rather than combative. The Gerry Mulligan Quartet with Chet Baker dropped the piano entirely, which forced the baritone and trumpet to imply the harmony through counterpoint, and produced the style's defining sound. Shorty Rogers, Shelly Manne, Jimmy Giuffre and Bud Shank are the other central figures. The style has been criticised, then and since, as polite and racially coded — the LA studio system was overwhelmingly white and the Black LA scene around Central Avenue was a distinct thing that got far less attention. Both criticisms have force. The music itself, taken on its own terms, is more rhythmically inventive than its reputation suggests.

musicalTraits.harmony: Clean bebop-derived changes with a taste for counterpoint over vertical density; some pieces borrow directly from fugue and canon procedures.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Light and buoyant rather than driving. Shelly Manne's playing is detailed and quiet, closer to a percussionist's approach than a swing drummer's.
musicalTraits.form: Heavily arranged: written introductions, interludes, backgrounds behind solos, and shaped endings. Less head–solos–head than anywhere else in 1950s jazz.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Piano-less quartets, flute and oboe doubling, baritone saxophone as a lead voice, occasional strings and woodwind sections.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Melodic and thematic, often developing a motif from the written material rather than running changes.
musicalTraits.timbre: Dry, close-recorded, transparent. Chet Baker's trumpet and Mulligan's baritone define the palette.

earMarkers: No piano at all in many groups — just horns, bass and drums
Two horns weaving separate lines around each other like a written duet
Flute, oboe or baritone saxophone carrying the melody
Everything sounding rehearsed rather than jammed
Quiet, detailed drumming with a lot of brushwork and rim sounds

keyFigures.name: Gerry Mulligan
keyFigures.why: The piano-less quartet was his idea and it defined the style's texture; also a first-rate contrapuntal writer.

keyFigures.name: Chet Baker
keyFigures.why: The style's lyrical voice — middle register, no vibrato, melodically simple and rhythmically subtle.

keyFigures.name: Shorty Rogers
keyFigures.why: The scene's most prolific arranger; his Giants sessions codified the West Coast small-band sound.

keyFigures.name: Shelly Manne
keyFigures.why: Redefined what a drummer could contribute texturally, and co-led the LA scene's most exploratory sessions.

keyFigures.name: Jimmy Giuffre
keyFigures.why: Pushed furthest out — drumless trios, folk-derived material, and by 1961 a chamber-free-jazz that predates most European improv.

genres.contested: Whether it is a real style or a marketing geography. Critics including many at the time argued 'West Coast jazz' described where records were made, not how they sounded — Ornette Coleman and Eric Dolphy were also in Los Angeles. This guide keeps it because the piano-less contrapuntal small group and the arranger-forward approach are a genuinely coherent set of choices.

genres.name: Hard Bop
genres.oneLine: Bebop with the blues and the church put back in — heavier, slower, and built to hit you in the chest.
genres.summary: By 1954 bebop had become a specialist's music and cool jazz had gone pale. Hard bop is the correction: the same harmonic language and the same quintet format, but slowed down, made bluesier, and reconnected to gospel and rhythm-and-blues. The tunes are catchier — often written by the band members themselves, with singable heads and memorable bass figures rather than abstract contrafacts. The drums get heavier, with a backbeat on 2 and 4 appearing regularly where swing drummers would have kept it on the cymbal. Piano comping picks up gospel voicings and repeated amen cadences. Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers, running from 1955 until his death in 1990, functioned as both the style's flagship and its university — Horace Silver, Benny Golson, Lee Morgan, Wayne Shorter, Freddie Hubbard, Keith Jarrett and dozens more came through it. Blue Note under Alfred Lion, with Rudy Van Gelder engineering and paid rehearsal time, gave the style a house sound that is still what most people mean when they picture a jazz record.

musicalTraits.harmony: Bebop changes plus explicit blues and gospel material — minor blues, modal vamps, IV–I plagal cadences lifted from church music.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Heavier and more grounded than bebop, with backbeats, Latin-tinged intros, and Blakey's press rolls and hard shuffle feels.
musicalTraits.form: Head–solos–head, but with composed introductions, interludes and shout choruses that make the records feel arranged.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Trumpet–tenor quintet is the default; sextets with trombone or alto are common. Organ and vibes appear at the edges.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Blues-saturated and rhythmically emphatic. Motivic repetition and worrying at a phrase are valued over pure line.
musicalTraits.timbre: Big, fat horn tones with more vibrato than bebop; Van Gelder's close-miked recording gives the drums and piano unusual weight.

earMarkers: Drums hitting hard on beats 2 and 4, not just riding the cymbal
Gospel-style church chords in the piano comping, with repeated amen-like cadences
Heads you can actually hum, often with a strong bass riff underneath
A drum roll that builds and crashes into the next soloist's entrance
Minor-key tunes with a Latin feel on the head that switches to swing for the solos

keyFigures.name: Art Blakey
keyFigures.why: Ran the Jazz Messengers for 35 years as both a band and a training system; his press roll and backbeat are the style's rhythmic signature.

keyFigures.name: Horace Silver
keyFigures.why: Wrote the tunes that defined the funky side of the style and made the piano a percussive, blues-drenched instrument.

keyFigures.name: Clifford Brown
keyFigures.why: The technical and lyrical model for every hard bop trumpeter; dead at 25 in 1956, which is why the recordings are so concentrated.

keyFigures.name: Cannonball Adderley
keyFigures.why: Carried the blues-and-joy side of the style to a large audience without softening the playing.

keyFigures.name: Lee Morgan
keyFigures.why: Blakey's most quotable soloist and the maker of the style's biggest commercial hit.

keyFigures.name: Sonny Rollins
keyFigures.why: Built solos by developing motifs across whole choruses — thematic improvisation as an explicit method.

genres.contested: Some writers treat hard bop and soul jazz as a single continuum rather than two genres, and there is no clean line — Horace Silver sits on both sides of it. This guide splits them at the point where the organ trio and the R&B backbeat become the format rather than a flavour. The label 'East Coast jazz' as an answer to West Coast is a critics' construction more than a musicians' one.

genres.name: Soul Jazz & Organ Trio
genres.oneLine: Jazz for the neighbourhood bar: Hammond organ, guitar, drums, a hard groove, and no interest in impressing critics.
genres.summary: The Hammond B-3 organ with a Leslie rotating speaker is the whole sound. One player covers bass with the pedals or the left hand, chords and melody with the right, and can swell the volume with a foot pedal in a way no piano can — which is why the organ trio needs no bassist and can fill a room. Jimmy Smith worked out the vocabulary in the mid-1950s and effectively created a job market: organ, guitar, drums, sometimes tenor, working the chitlin' circuit and neighbourhood taverns rather than concert halls. The music is groove-first, blues-based, often built on simple vamps and 12-bar forms, with long solos and an audience that responds out loud. It was hugely popular and largely dismissed by the jazz press at the time as commercial, which says more about the press than the music. Everything in later jazz-funk, acid jazz and hip-hop-sampled jazz runs back through here — a huge proportion of sampled jazz breaks come from soul jazz records.

musicalTraits.harmony: Blues and simple functional changes, gospel plagal cadences, and long single-chord vamps. Harmonic ambition is deliberately not the point.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Shuffle and backbeat feels drawn from rhythm and blues, with the drummer often playing a boogaloo or a hard 12/8.
musicalTraits.form: 12-bar blues, simple riff tunes, and modal vamps stretched out for extended solos. Head arrangements, minimal writing.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Hammond B-3 through a Leslie cabinet, electric guitar, drums, and often tenor saxophone. No upright bass — the organ covers it.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Long, riff-driven, and openly crowd-pleasing. Repetition and building intensity matter more than harmonic navigation.
musicalTraits.timbre: The Leslie speaker's swirl is the defining colour, plus hollow-body guitar with a warm, unhurried attack and a big-toned tenor.

earMarkers: Hammond organ with that swirling, rotating speaker sound
No double bass — the bass line is being played by the organist's left hand or feet
A hard backbeat you could dance to, closer to R&B than to swing
Long stretches sitting on one chord while the solo builds
Audible crowd noise — a lot of these were recorded live in bars

keyFigures.name: Jimmy Smith
keyFigures.why: Invented the modern jazz organ vocabulary — bass lines in the left hand, bebop lines in the right — and created the format.

keyFigures.name: Grant Green
keyFigures.why: The most rhythmically pure single-note guitarist of the style; almost never played chords in solos.

keyFigures.name: Stanley Turrentine
keyFigures.why: The definitive soul jazz tenor tone — huge, warm, blues-first.

keyFigures.name: Jack McDuff
keyFigures.why: Ran the hardest-grooving of the working organ bands and gave George Benson his first job.

keyFigures.name: Ramsey Lewis
keyFigures.why: Proved the piano trio could do the same job, and took soul jazz into the pop charts in 1965.

genres.contested: Where hard bop ends and soul jazz begins. Horace Silver, Cannonball Adderley and Lee Morgan sit on both sides. Some writers also fold Ramsey Lewis and the piano-based groove records into a separate 'crossover' category. The genre's low critical standing at the time has been substantially revised.

genres.name: Modal Jazz
genres.oneLine: Take away most of the chords and see what a soloist does with the space.
genres.summary: Bebop and hard bop hand the improviser a chord every two beats; modal jazz might hand them one scale for sixteen bars. The reduction is the innovation. With the harmony slowed almost to a stop, a soloist can no longer succeed by outlining changes accurately, and has to build a line out of melodic shape, motif and colour instead. George Russell's Lydian Chromatic Concept, published in 1953, gave the idea a theoretical frame; Miles Davis's 'Milestones' in 1958 and Kind of Blue in 1959 gave it a sound. The consequences show up everywhere: quartal voicings in the piano (stacked fourths, which are ambiguous about what key you are in), pedal points in the bass, drummers freed from marking chord changes and able to play texture, and modes borrowed from outside the major/minor system. Coltrane pushed it further and harder than Davis did, turning single-chord vamps into ecstatic marathons, and by way of that the style opens directly into spiritual jazz and free playing.

musicalTraits.harmony: Static or very slow-moving. One scale or mode held for long stretches, with quartal and suspended voicings that avoid stating a clear tonal centre.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Freed from chord-marking. Bass often plays pedal points or ostinatos; drums play colour and wave-shape rather than navigation.
musicalTraits.form: Long sections over a single mode, sometimes with a second mode as contrast. Forms can be irregular lengths because they are not tied to song structure.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Standard quintet or sextet, but the piano's role changes fundamentally — texture and colour over functional comping.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Melodic and motivic. With no changes to navigate, the soloist must generate interest from shape, repetition, register and intensity.
musicalTraits.timbre: Space becomes audible. Bill Evans' voicings and Coltrane's overtone-rich upper register are the two ends of the style's colour range.

earMarkers: The harmony sits still — you can wait a long time for the chord to change
Piano chords built from stacked fourths, which sound open and unresolved
A bass note held or repeated under everything (a pedal point)
Melodies that sound slightly foreign because the scale isn't ordinary major or minor
A soloist building intensity by repetition rather than by moving through chords

keyFigures.name: Miles Davis
keyFigures.why: Made the theoretical idea audible and commercially enormous with Kind of Blue in 1959.

keyFigures.name: John Coltrane
keyFigures.why: Took modal frameworks to their limit — long vamps played at maximum intensity, which is where free jazz starts for him.

keyFigures.name: Bill Evans
keyFigures.why: Supplied the voicing language, borrowed partly from Ravel and Debussy, that makes modal harmony sound the way it does.

keyFigures.name: George Russell
keyFigures.why: Wrote the Lydian Chromatic Concept, the theoretical framework that gave modal thinking a vocabulary.

keyFigures.name: McCoy Tyner
keyFigures.why: Turned quartal voicings into a percussive, pentatonic-driven style that became the default sound of modal piano.

keyFigures.name: Herbie Hancock
keyFigures.why: Wrote modal pieces with ambiguous, floating harmony that avoid both functional resolution and static vamps.

genres.contested: Whether modal jazz is a genre or a technique. Almost every post-1960 style uses modal devices, and albums like Kind of Blue get filed as modal, cool, or post-bop depending on the writer. Whether Kind of Blue is modal jazz or a modal-flavoured hard bop record is a genuinely live argument.

genres.name: Third Stream
genres.oneLine: Composers trying to get classical form and jazz improvisation into the same piece without either one winning.
genres.summary: Gunther Schuller coined the term in a 1957 lecture at Brandeis University, describing a third stream flowing between the classical and jazz mainstreams. The premise: use the compositional resources of Western art music — twelve-tone rows, fugue, extended form, orchestral instrumentation — while keeping improvisation as a live element rather than decoration. The Modern Jazz Quartet under John Lewis had been circling the idea since 1952 with baroque counterpoint over blues; Schuller, Charles Mingus, George Russell and Jimmy Giuffre pushed it further. The problems are obvious in hindsight and were obvious then: classical players could not improvise convincingly, jazz players found the written material stiff, and a lot of the results sound like two musics politely taking turns. But the successful examples are genuinely strange and good, and the idea did not die — it re-emerges in ECM's chamber jazz, in Anthony Braxton's compositional systems, and in almost every contemporary large-ensemble writer. Schuller later expanded the term to mean any fusion of an improvised and a notated tradition, not only European ones.

musicalTraits.harmony: Twelve-tone and freely atonal writing alongside jazz harmony; polytonality and unresolved dissonance used structurally.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Often deliberately un-swung in the composed sections, with metric modulation and irregular meters, then a swing feel entering with the improvisation.
musicalTraits.form: Extended, through-composed structures — sonata-like development, fugue, theme and variations — with improvised sections written into the architecture.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Jazz group plus string quartet, chamber orchestra, or full symphony; also the Modern Jazz Quartet's austere vibes-piano-bass-drums.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Constrained and located — the soloist improvises within a specified section, sometimes on a row or a set of pitches rather than changes.
musicalTraits.timbre: Concert-hall clarity and dynamic range. Strings, woodwinds and percussion used for colour in ways rare elsewhere in jazz.

earMarkers: Strings or woodwinds that are clearly a classical section, not a pop string sweetening
Passages of counterpoint that sound like Bach, followed by a swinging solo
Dissonance that never resolves, used on purpose
Long pieces in several distinct movements rather than head–solos–head
An audible seam where the written part stops and improvisation begins

keyFigures.name: Gunther Schuller
keyFigures.why: Named the movement, wrote much of its repertoire, and later wrote the two-volume history of jazz that shaped how it is taught.

keyFigures.name: John Lewis
keyFigures.why: The Modern Jazz Quartet applied fugal and rondo procedures to blues material for four decades without gimmickry.

keyFigures.name: Charles Mingus
keyFigures.why: His extended works use classical scale and ambition while remaining rooted in blues and gospel; he rejected the label but fits the description.

keyFigures.name: George Russell
keyFigures.why: Combined a rigorous theoretical system with big-band writing that neither classical nor jazz orthodoxy could claim.

keyFigures.name: Jimmy Giuffre
keyFigures.why: His 1961 trio with Paul Bley and Steve Swallow is chamber music and free improvisation at the same time.

genres.contested: Whether it is a genre, a project, or a failure. Many musicians it describes — Mingus above all — rejected the label. Schuller himself later widened the definition so far that it arguably stopped naming anything specific. Critics of the term argue it presumes classical music is a separate, higher stream that jazz must be married into.

genres.name: Post-Bop
genres.oneLine: The music of players who absorbed free jazz without abandoning form — ambiguous, floating, still structured.
genres.summary: By the mid-1960s a group of musicians had heard Ornette Coleman and Cecil Taylor and did not want to go all the way, but could not go back either. Post-bop is what they built. The forms are still there but stretched — 22 bars instead of 32, sections of irregular length, tunes that never quite resolve. The harmony floats: chords with ambiguous function, key centres that shift without announcing themselves, melodies that imply several possible tonalities. The rhythm section becomes genuinely interactive rather than supportive — the Miles Davis Second Great Quintet with Hancock, Carter and Williams played 'time, no changes', keeping a pulse while treating the harmony as negotiable, and Williams could imply three tempos at once. Wayne Shorter's compositions are the central body of writing: short, enigmatic heads with harmony that resists analysis. Andrew Hill, Bobby Hutcherson, Joe Henderson and Herbie Hancock make up most of the rest. It is still the default language of conservatory-trained modern jazz, which is why the term also gets used loosely for anything mainstream and post-1960.

musicalTraits.harmony: Functionally ambiguous. Slash chords, unresolved suspensions, modal interchange, and progressions that move by step or third rather than by fifth.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Elastic. The pulse is present but the group can imply double time, half time, or a different meter simultaneously; the drummer is a co-improviser.
musicalTraits.form: Irregular section lengths, forms that don't loop cleanly, and pieces where the solo section differs structurally from the head.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Quintet and sextet formats; vibraphone becomes prominent, and the piano sometimes drops out entirely.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Freer relationship to the written harmony — playing 'outside' deliberately and resolving back, or ignoring the changes while keeping the form.
musicalTraits.timbre: Cooler and more transparent than hard bop. Space and dynamics are compositional elements.

earMarkers: Chords that never settle — you can't tell what key the tune is in
The drummer commenting and disrupting rather than keeping steady time
Forms that don't come around when you expect them to
Solos that go deliberately 'wrong' against the harmony, then snap back
Heads that are short, strange, and hard to hum

keyFigures.name: Wayne Shorter
keyFigures.why: Wrote the style's core repertoire — harmonically slippery pieces that are still being played and still resist easy analysis.

keyFigures.name: Herbie Hancock
keyFigures.why: Developed a comping approach that suggests rather than states harmony, and wrote the floating pieces that define the sound.

keyFigures.name: Tony Williams
keyFigures.why: Joined Miles at 17 and rebuilt the drummer's role as an equal improviser who can move the time without losing it.

keyFigures.name: Andrew Hill
keyFigures.why: The most structurally radical of the Blue Note post-bop writers; his forms are asymmetric in ways that still sound unusual.

keyFigures.name: Joe Henderson
keyFigures.why: Moved between inside and outside playing more fluently than almost anyone, on both hard bop and avant-garde dates.

keyFigures.name: Bobby Hutcherson
keyFigures.why: Made the vibraphone a colour instrument for ambiguous harmony rather than a novelty.

genres.contested: The term is used two incompatible ways: narrowly for the mid-1960s Blue Note/Miles quintet music described here, and broadly for any acoustic jazz made after bebop that isn't free. Some writers file Kind of Blue and much of the 1970s mainstream here too. This guide uses the narrow definition and says so.

genres.name: Afro-Cuban & Latin Jazz
genres.oneLine: Jazz harmony and soloing built on Cuban clave instead of swing — the rhythm section is doing something completely different.
genres.summary: The change is rhythmic and it is total. Swing divides the beat into a lilting triplet feel; Afro-Cuban music divides it evenly and organises everything around clave, a two-bar asymmetric pattern (three strokes in one bar, two in the other) that every other part must align with. Get the clave backwards and the whole band sounds wrong to anyone who knows. Layer on top the tumbao bass pattern that anticipates the downbeat rather than landing on it, the montuno piano figure, congas, timbales, bongos, cowbell — and you have a rhythm section that is polyrhythmic by design rather than by accident. Dizzy Gillespie and Cuban percussionist Chano Pozo made the fusion explicit in 1947 with 'Manteca' and 'Cubana Be, Cubana Bop', and Machito's orchestra with arranger Mario Bauzá had been doing it in New York since 1940. Later waves brought Brazilian, Puerto Rican and Panamanian currents, and by the 1970s the Fania-era salsa scene and jazz were sharing personnel constantly. The African retentions in Cuban music were less interrupted than in the US, which is part of why the meeting felt like a reunion.

musicalTraits.harmony: Jazz harmony largely intact — bebop changes, modal vamps, and montuno progressions that cycle a short chord sequence indefinitely.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Clave-organised, with even (straight) eighth notes rather than swung ones. Tumbao bass anticipates beat 1, and multiple percussion parts interlock.
musicalTraits.form: Often two-part: a written, arranged section followed by a montuno — an open vamp for solos, mambo horn riffs and percussion features.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Full jazz horn section plus congas, timbales, bongos, güiro, claves, cowbell. Piano plays montuno figures rather than comping freely.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Bebop-derived soloing over vamps, plus percussion soloing as a featured element in its own right.
musicalTraits.timbre: Bright, brassy and dense. Percussion is foregrounded rather than treated as accompaniment.

earMarkers: Even, straight eighth notes instead of the loping swing feel
A repeating two-bar pattern (clave) that everything else lines up against
Congas and timbales, not just a drum kit
The bass landing just before the downbeat rather than on it
A long open section where the band vamps on two chords and the percussion takes over

keyFigures.name: Mario Bauzá
keyFigures.why: Machito's musical director and the person who actually engineered the meeting of Cuban rhythm and jazz orchestration.

keyFigures.name: Chano Pozo
keyFigures.why: Brought authentic Afro-Cuban drumming and its religious repertoire into Gillespie's band; murdered in 1948 at 33.

keyFigures.name: Dizzy Gillespie
keyFigures.why: The bebop figure who insisted the rhythmic connection mattered and had the platform to prove it.

keyFigures.name: Tito Puente
keyFigures.why: Bridged mambo dance music and jazz for five decades with formidable arranging chops.

keyFigures.name: Eddie Palmieri
keyFigures.why: Brought McCoy Tyner's harmonic density and free-jazz edges into salsa without losing the dance floor.

keyFigures.name: Chucho Valdés
keyFigures.why: Led Irakere in Cuba, fusing Yoruba batá drumming with post-bop harmony under conditions of near-total isolation from the US scene.

genres.contested: Whether 'Latin jazz' is one genre or a shorthand for several unrelated ones. Cuban-derived, Brazilian, Puerto Rican and Argentine jazz traditions have different rhythmic bases and grouping them can obscure more than it explains. This guide separates the Brazilian stream out for that reason.

genres.name: Bossa Nova & Brazilian Jazz
genres.oneLine: Samba played quietly, with jazz harmony and a voice barely above speech.
genres.summary: Bossa nova is samba with the volume and the percussion battery removed and the harmony made much more complicated. João Gilberto worked out the guitar pattern — a syncopated thumb-and-fingers figure that implies a whole samba percussion section on one instrument — and a way of singing almost without projection, so close to the microphone that it sounds like someone thinking out loud. Antônio Carlos Jobim wrote the songs, with chromatic inner voices and chord movements that come as much from Debussy and Chopin as from any Brazilian source. Vinicius de Moraes wrote many of the lyrics. It arrived in the US in 1962 through Charlie Byrd and Stan Getz, and 'The Girl from Ipanema' turned it into a global commercial phenomenon so complete that it became lounge wallpaper, which has damaged its reputation ever since. Underneath the easy-listening reception there is a serious body of work, and the wider Brazilian instrumental tradition — Hermeto Pascoal, Egberto Gismonti, Airto Moreira, Milton Nascimento — pushed far past bossa into territory that fed 1970s fusion directly.

musicalTraits.harmony: The most harmonically complex popular song repertoire of its era: chromatic descending inner lines, altered dominants, and modulations that arrive without warning.
musicalTraits.rhythm: The bossa guitar pattern displaces accents across two bars, derived from samba but stripped to essentials. Even eighths, soft dynamics, brushes or light sticks on the kit.
musicalTraits.form: Song forms, often through-composed and irregular rather than 32-bar AABA. Instrumental versions extend them with solo choruses.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Nylon-string guitar, voice, piano, bass, drums with brushes; often flute or saxophone. Percussion is minimal compared with samba.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Restrained and melodic in bossa proper; the later samba-jazz and Brazilian instrumental scenes are far more virtuosic.
musicalTraits.timbre: Soft, warm, close-miked. Gilberto's near-whispered singing and the nylon-string guitar define the palette.

earMarkers: One nylon-string guitar playing a syncopated pattern that implies a whole percussion section
Singing that is quiet, conversational and almost never held out
Chords that shift in unexpected directions under a very simple melody
Even eighth notes with no swing lilt
Drums played with brushes and a rim-click, kept very low in the mix

keyFigures.name: João Gilberto
keyFigures.why: Invented both the guitar pattern and the vocal delivery; without him bossa nova does not exist as a sound.

keyFigures.name: Antônio Carlos Jobim
keyFigures.why: Wrote the repertoire, and wrote it with a harmonic sophistication that made it durable jazz material.

keyFigures.name: Stan Getz
keyFigures.why: The American who carried it to a mass audience, with a tone light enough not to crush the material.

keyFigures.name: Hermeto Pascoal
keyFigures.why: The Brazilian tradition at its most unrestrained — folk forms, free improvisation, and sounds made from anything at hand.

keyFigures.name: Airto Moreira
keyFigures.why: Brought Brazilian percussion into American fusion, appearing on Bitches Brew and with Weather Report and Return to Forever.

keyFigures.name: Egberto Gismonti
keyFigures.why: Combined Brazilian folk material, classical technique and improvisation, mostly through ECM.

genres.contested: Whether bossa nova is jazz at all. In Brazil it is classified as popular song, and Brazilian musicians often find the American framing of it as a jazz style distorting. Its 1960s American reception also flattened a sharply defined art movement into background music, a reading that Brazilian critics have pushed back on for sixty years.

genres.name: Ethio-Jazz
genres.oneLine: Ethiopian five-note modes and jazz-funk instrumentation, producing a sound that seems to be in a minor key and a major key at once.
genres.summary: Ethiopian traditional music uses a system of pentatonic modes called qignit, of which four are common — tizita, bati, ambassel and anchihoye. They are five-note scales with wide intervals, and to ears trained on Western music they sound simultaneously mournful and unresolved. Mulatu Astatke, who studied in London and at Berklee in Boston and had absorbed Latin jazz along the way, put those modes over jazz and funk instrumentation — vibraphone, electric bass, organ, horn sections, congas — and called the result Ethio-jazz. The rhythmic feel is its own thing: a loping, slightly dragging groove often in 6/8 or a swung 4, quite unlike either American funk or Cuban clave. The music flourished under Haile Selassie's later years, then was largely shut down by the Derg regime's curfews and nationalisation of the record industry after 1974. It was rediscovered internationally through the Éthiopiques reissue series, launched in 1997 by Francis Falceto on Buda Musique, and Jim Jarmusch's use of Astatke's music in Broken Flowers in 2005.

musicalTraits.harmony: Built on pentatonic qignit modes rather than functional harmony. Chords are often ambiguous or drone-like, supporting the mode rather than moving through changes.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Loping and slightly behind, frequently in compound meters. Neither swing nor clave — the feel derives from Ethiopian dance rhythms like the chik chika.
musicalTraits.form: Short repeating structures with extended vamps for solos; horn riffs stated and restated rather than developed.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Vibraphone (Astatke's signature), electric organ, electric bass, horn section, congas and kit; sometimes the traditional krar and masenqo.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Modal soloing within the qignit, often quite short. The groove and the mode, rather than solo display, carry the music.
musicalTraits.timbre: Warm, slightly murky analogue recording; vibraphone and Farfisa-style organ against a reedy horn section.

earMarkers: A five-note scale with big gaps in it that sounds neither major nor minor
Vibraphone playing lead lines over an electric bass groove
A groove that drags slightly behind the beat rather than pushing
Horn riffs that repeat without developing, hypnotically
Organ tones that sound closer to 1960s garage rock than to jazz

keyFigures.name: Mulatu Astatke
keyFigures.why: Named and defined the style; the only person who deliberately set out to fuse Ethiopian modes with jazz as a project.

keyFigures.name: Girma Bèyènè
keyFigures.why: Arranger on much of the Addis golden-age catalogue and a distinctive singer in his own right.

keyFigures.name: Mahmoud Ahmed
keyFigures.why: The great vocalist of the era; his Erè Mèla Mèla was the record that broke Ethiopian music in Europe in the mid-1980s.

keyFigures.name: Getatchew Mekurya
keyFigures.why: Adapted the shellela, a sung Ethiopian war chant, to saxophone, arriving at something that sounds like free jazz by a completely different route.

keyFigures.name: Hailu Mergia
keyFigures.why: Led the Walias Band, then spent decades driving a taxi in Washington DC before his rediscovery.

genres.contested: Whether Ethio-jazz names a genre or one man's project. Astatke coined the term for his own music, and much of what gets filed under it — Mahmoud Ahmed's vocal records, the Walias Band's instrumentals — is Ethiopian popular music with horns rather than a jazz-derived fusion. The Éthiopiques series bundled all of it together for a European audience.

genres.name: J-Jazz
genres.oneLine: Japanese players taking modal and spiritual jazz somewhere harder, denser and more audiophile-recorded than anyone in America was.
genres.summary: Japan had a jazz scene from the 1920s, but the thing worth hearing starts in the late 1960s, when a generation of players stopped copying American records and started producing something with its own weight. The reference points are Coltrane's quartet, Blue Note post-bop and free jazz, but the results are distinct: harder-edged, often darker, with a taste for extended modal vamps, unusual instrumentation, and a physical intensity in the playing. Yosuke Yamashita's trio played free jazz with the violence of a rock band. Masabumi Kikuchi and Terumasa Hino went deep into electric fusion. Masahiko Togashi built a percussion language after a spinal injury left him unable to use his legs. Traditional Japanese instruments and materials appear — shakuhachi, koto, folk melodies — but usually as structure rather than decoration. Crucially, the independent labels, above all Three Blind Mice, founded in 1970 by Takeshi Fujii with the explicit ambition of being 'the Blue Note of Japan', recorded the music with extraordinary audio quality, which is part of why the reissue market went so hard for it after the BBE compilations from 2018 onward.

musicalTraits.harmony: Modal and post-bop derived, with a marked preference for minor modes, quartal voicings and long static vamps.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Often heavier and more insistent than American models; rock and funk backbeats appear alongside free time and traditional Japanese metrical ideas.
musicalTraits.form: Extended pieces, frequently side-long, with slow builds from near-silence to collective intensity.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Standard jazz groups plus electric keyboards, and occasionally shakuhachi, koto, biwa or taiko.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Physical and sustained. The free wing plays at very high energy; the modal wing favours long, patient development.
musicalTraits.timbre: Exceptional recording quality — Three Blind Mice and Nippon Columbia's engineers captured bass and drums with unusual depth and dynamic range.

earMarkers: Modal vamps held far longer than an American record of the same period would
Bass and drums recorded with startling clarity and presence
Piano attacked percussively, sometimes almost violently
Traditional Japanese instruments used structurally rather than as exotic colour
Long slow builds from near-silence to full intensity across ten minutes or more

keyFigures.name: Terumasa Hino
keyFigures.why: The most internationally visible Japanese jazz musician of the era; moved from hard bop through free to electric fusion.

keyFigures.name: Yosuke Yamashita
keyFigures.why: His drummerless-free trio played with a physical ferocity that made European free-jazz audiences take Japan seriously in the 1970s.

keyFigures.name: Masabumi Kikuchi
keyFigures.why: Moved between Gil Evans' orchestra, electric fusion and, much later, an extremely spare ECM trio; one of the most restless careers in the music.

keyFigures.name: Masahiko Togashi
keyFigures.why: Rebuilt his entire approach to the kit after a 1969 injury, producing a uniquely spacious percussion language.

keyFigures.name: Sadao Watanabe
keyFigures.why: Studied at Berklee and returned to teach; the central populariser and educator of the Japanese scene.

keyFigures.name: Toshiko Akiyoshi
keyFigures.why: The first Japanese musician to break through in the US, and a major big-band composer who wrote Japanese material into the idiom.

genres.contested: Whether 'J-jazz' is a genre or a nationality with a reissue market attached. The term was popularised by European compilers in the 2010s rather than by Japanese musicians, and it lumps free jazz, spiritual jazz, fusion and hard bop together on the basis of geography. This guide keeps it because the scene had its own labels, its own recording aesthetic and a distinct set of shared reference points — but the objection is fair.

genres.name: European Free Improvisation
genres.oneLine: Improvisation that cut its ties to jazz entirely — no tunes, no pulse, no blues, no American vocabulary.
genres.summary: American free jazz kept a great deal: a rhythmic pulse most of the time, a blues sensibility, the sound of the saxophone as a voice, and often a head to start from. European improvisers in the mid-1960s decided to cut all of it. Derek Bailey called the result 'non-idiomatic improvisation' and meant it as a technical description — music that deliberately avoids belonging to any style, including free jazz. In practice that means extended techniques, extreme dynamic range, silence used structurally, and a rejection of anything that would let a listener predict the next event. The scenes were national and distinct: London around the Spontaneous Music Ensemble, Bailey, Evan Parker and the Incus label, favouring quiet, fast, detailed interaction; Amsterdam around Misha Mengelberg, Han Bennink and the Instant Composers Pool, full of theatre, absurdity and sudden collapses into Monk tunes; Wuppertal and Berlin around Peter Brötzmann, at maximum volume and maximum density. Politics were explicit — several of these musicians framed the work as a rejection of American cultural dominance and of the market itself, and set up their own labels to prove it.

musicalTraits.harmony: None in any functional sense. Pitch is used as texture and colour; consonance appears as one option among many, never as a resting place.
musicalTraits.rhythm: No steady pulse. Rhythm exists as gesture, density and interruption. When a groove appears it is usually a joke or a quotation.
musicalTraits.form: Real-time and emergent. Pieces begin and end when the players decide; recordings are often single unbroken improvisations.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Anything. Prepared and amplified instruments, homemade devices, objects, voice. Bailey used amplification and volume pedals as compositional tools.
musicalTraits.improvisation: The entire content. Listening and response operate on a very fast timescale, closer to conversation than to soloing.
musicalTraits.timbre: The primary parameter. Multiphonics, circular breathing, scraped strings, feedback, near-inaudible sounds next to sudden violence.

earMarkers: No steady beat anywhere, and no melody that repeats
Instruments making sounds you can't identify — scrapes, squeaks, air, feedback
Long silences used as part of the music, not as mistakes
Volume that jumps from almost nothing to overwhelming without warning
Players reacting to each other within a fraction of a second, like fast conversation

keyFigures.name: Derek Bailey
keyFigures.why: Theorised and practised non-idiomatic improvisation more rigorously than anyone; also wrote the movement's key book.

keyFigures.name: Evan Parker
keyFigures.why: Developed a circular-breathing, multiphonic solo soprano language that has no antecedent in jazz saxophone.

keyFigures.name: Peter Brötzmann
keyFigures.why: The German wing's ferocity in one player; Machine Gun in 1968 remains a hard line in the sand.

keyFigures.name: Han Bennink
keyFigures.why: Brought physical comedy and total unpredictability to the kit, and played anything in the room as an instrument.

keyFigures.name: Misha Mengelberg
keyFigures.why: Ran the Dutch scene's mix of rigour and absurdism, and kept Monk and Herbie Nichols alive inside free improvisation.

keyFigures.name: John Stevens
keyFigures.why: The Spontaneous Music Ensemble's organiser, whose 'insect music' aesthetic prioritised listening over projection.

genres.contested: Whether it belongs in a jazz lineage at all. Bailey argued explicitly that free improvisation is not a jazz style, and many practitioners reject the connection. The counter-argument is genealogical rather than musical: nearly all the first generation came out of playing jazz, and the break only makes sense in relation to what it broke from.

genres.name: Free Jazz
genres.oneLine: Jazz that abandoned the chord changes, and then, in some hands, the beat and the form as well.
genres.summary: The chord sequence had been the container for jazz improvisation for forty years. Free jazz threw it out. Ornette Coleman's quartet — no piano, so nothing stating harmony — played tunes with clear melodies and then improvised on the melodic and emotional content rather than a fixed harmonic grid, keeping a pulse. Cecil Taylor came from the other side, with a percussive, dense, atonal piano attack rooted in twentieth-century composition as much as in jazz. Albert Ayler kept marches, folk melodies and hymns as raw material, then obliterated them with a huge shuddering tone and mass collective improvisation. Coltrane arrived in 1965 with Ascension and took his audience with him. Common features: no pre-set changes, frequently no fixed meter, collective rather than sequential improvisation, and an expanded idea of acceptable sound — squeals, overtones, screams. The reception was hostile in a way that is hard to overstate; musicians lost work over it. The politics were inseparable, running alongside the civil rights and Black Power movements, and several key figures framed the music explicitly in those terms.

musicalTraits.harmony: No pre-agreed progression. Pitch centres emerge and dissolve; players may follow a melodic contour or a mood rather than a key.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Pulse is optional. Ornette's groups mostly keep one; Taylor and Ayler's often abandon meter entirely for waves of density.
musicalTraits.form: Frequently a stated theme, then open collective improvisation, then a return. Duration is determined by the performance, not the form.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Often piano-less, so no instrument is fixing the harmony. Double bassists sometimes doubled; two drummers appear regularly.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Simultaneous and collective. Everyone can lead at once; the New Orleans front line comes back in radically altered form.
musicalTraits.timbre: Enormously expanded — overblowing, altissimo screams, split tones, vocalised cries. Sound as expression, not as tone production.

earMarkers: No repeating chord pattern to follow — the harmony never comes around
Several players soloing at once instead of taking turns
Saxophones screaming, honking and producing more than one note at a time
The beat disappearing entirely for long stretches
A clear, almost naive melody at the start and end of something otherwise chaotic

keyFigures.name: Ornette Coleman
keyFigures.why: Removed the chord changes while keeping melody and pulse; his 1959–61 Atlantic records are the founding statement.

keyFigures.name: Cecil Taylor
keyFigures.why: Built a percussive, atonal, physically overwhelming piano language from a different starting point than Coleman's.

keyFigures.name: Albert Ayler
