keyFigures.why: Used hymns, marches and folk tunes as launch material and a vast vibrato-drenched tone; the most emotionally extreme voice in the music.

keyFigures.name: John Coltrane
keyFigures.why: His move into free playing after 1965 gave the style credibility and an audience it could not otherwise have reached.

keyFigures.name: Sun Ra
keyFigures.why: Ran the Arkestra from the mid-1950s with a mix of big-band writing, electronics, free improvisation and cosmology all at once.

keyFigures.name: Archie Shepp
keyFigures.why: Tied the music explicitly to Black political struggle in his writing and speech as well as his playing.

genres.contested: Whether 'free jazz' is one thing. Ornette Coleman's melodic, pulse-keeping music and Cecil Taylor's atonal density have almost nothing in common technically, and Coleman himself disliked the term. 'The New Thing' was the period label; 'energy music' names only one wing of it.

genres.name: AACM & Great Black Music
genres.oneLine: Free jazz that got organised — a musicians' collective that added composition, silence, theatre and a hundred small instruments.
genres.summary: The Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians was founded in Chicago in 1965 by Muhal Richard Abrams and others as a self-governing organisation: members ran their own concerts, taught a free music school, and refused to depend on club owners or record companies. That structure produced a music distinct from New York free jazz. Where the New York scene favoured continuous high-energy blowing, the AACM built pieces with composed sections, extreme dynamic contrast, and long stretches of near-silence. The Art Ensemble of Chicago's slogan, 'Great Black Music, Ancient to the Future', announces the scope: field hollers, marches, bebop, free improvisation and African percussion inside a single performance, often in face paint and costume, with theatre as an explicit element. 'Little instruments' — bells, whistles, gongs, toys, bicycle horns, anything — became a signature, and members routinely play four or five instruments each. Anthony Braxton took the compositional side furthest, into diagrammatically titled works and multi-orchestra pieces. A parallel collective, BAG, formed in St. Louis in 1968, and both fed the New York loft scene in the 1970s.

musicalTraits.harmony: Ranges from fully atonal to plain diatonic depending on the section. Harmony is a compositional choice made per passage, not a governing system.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Anything from strict written meter to free time to processional march. Silence is treated as a rhythmic value.
musicalTraits.form: Composed multi-section works, graphic and verbal scores, and structures that allocate freedom differently in each part.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Multi-instrumentalism as standard, plus a percussion battery of small instruments. Contrabass clarinet, sopranino saxophone, bassoon and non-Western instruments all appear.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Inside a designed frame. The question is usually 'what kind of freedom does this section have', not 'is this free'.
musicalTraits.timbre: Extreme range and extreme contrast — a bicycle horn next to a bass saxophone next to four minutes of almost nothing.

earMarkers: Very long quiet passages where almost nothing happens, then sudden density
Bells, whistles, gongs and toys used as seriously as the horns
One player switching between four or five instruments within a piece
Abrupt swerves between styles — a march, then chaos, then a bebop line
Composed written sections that clearly aren't improvised

keyFigures.name: Muhal Richard Abrams
keyFigures.why: Co-founded the AACM and ran the Experimental Band that trained most of its first generation.

keyFigures.name: Roscoe Mitchell
keyFigures.why: Sound in 1966 is the first AACM record and one of the first jazz records to use silence as a structural material.

keyFigures.name: Anthony Braxton
keyFigures.why: Built the largest and most systematic compositional apparatus in the music, while also playing standards and solo saxophone.

keyFigures.name: Art Ensemble of Chicago
keyFigures.why: The style's public face: theatre, costume, little instruments, and a repertoire spanning the whole history of Black music.

keyFigures.name: Henry Threadgill
keyFigures.why: Wrote for unusual fixed instrumentations — tuba and cello ensembles, two guitars, two tubas — with a compositional rigour that won a Pulitzer in 2016.

keyFigures.name: Julius Hemphill
keyFigures.why: The central figure of St. Louis's BAG and founder of the World Saxophone Quartet.

genres.contested: Whether the AACM constitutes a genre or an institution whose members made very different music. Braxton, Threadgill and the Art Ensemble share an approach to structure and self-organisation more than a sound. 'Great Black Music' is the Art Ensemble's own framing and is broader than any style label.

genres.name: Spiritual Jazz
genres.oneLine: Modal jazz aimed at transcendence — drones, chanting, harps, and long ecstatic builds that function as devotion.
genres.summary: A Love Supreme in 1965 established the template: a suite structured as a religious offering, with a chanted mantra, a bass ostinato functioning as a drone, and a build to ecstatic release. What follows takes those elements and adds the instruments and modes of Indian, African and Middle Eastern devotional music — tanpura drones, harp, sitar, hand percussion, bells, kalimba, voices chanting in unison. Alice Coltrane brought the harp and Hindu devotional practice; Pharoah Sanders combined near-nursery-rhyme melodies with tenor playing at the edge of what the horn can produce; Sun Ra was already there by a different route. Detroit's Tribe collective and Strata-East in New York provided the institutional base — artist-run labels making records that no major would touch, which is also why originals are so scarce and so expensive. The category is largely retrospective: it was assembled by DJs, reissue compilers and record collectors from the 1990s onward, and the musicians themselves generally just said they were playing jazz. That does not make it unreal, but it is worth knowing.

musicalTraits.harmony: Modal and drone-based. Long pedal points, pentatonic and Eastern-derived modes, and simple two-chord frames that can be sustained indefinitely.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Ostinato-driven, often in 6/8 or 3/4, with hand percussion layered over the kit. Tempo is usually stable but not the focus.
musicalTraits.form: Suites and long-form pieces with distinct movements; a common shape is calm statement, escalation to collective intensity, and return.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Saxophones and piano plus harp, tanpura, sitar, oud, bells, shakers, kalimba, choral voices, and occasionally strings.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Long, cumulative and intensity-driven rather than harmonically navigational; overblowing and multiphonics used as devotional expression.
musicalTraits.timbre: Reverb-heavy, wide, with drones underneath. The harp and bells give the style its distinctive shimmer.

earMarkers: A drone or repeated bass figure that holds under the whole piece
Voices chanting a short phrase over and over
Harp, bells, or hand percussion where you would expect a piano
Saxophone playing that goes from gentle melody to screaming and back
Pieces built as slow builds over ten or fifteen minutes, structured like a rite

keyFigures.name: John Coltrane
keyFigures.why: A Love Supreme gave the idiom its structure, its intent and its permission.

keyFigures.name: Alice Coltrane
keyFigures.why: Brought the harp, Hindu devotional practice and string orchestration into jazz and made a body of work nobody has matched.

keyFigures.name: Pharoah Sanders
keyFigures.why: Paired simple, almost childlike melodies with extreme overblowing — the style's characteristic contrast in a single player.

keyFigures.name: Sun Ra
keyFigures.why: Was doing cosmology, robes and collective ritual a decade before the term existed.

keyFigures.name: Don Cherry
keyFigures.why: Took the impulse global — Turkish, Indian, Malian and Scandinavian folk material inside an improvising frame.

keyFigures.name: Doug Carn
keyFigures.why: With vocalist Jean Carn, made the most song-based version of the style for Black Jazz Records.

genres.contested: Whether it is a genre at all. The term was constructed retrospectively by compilers and collectors, largely from the 1990s onward, and the musicians described by it saw themselves as playing modal or free jazz with religious intent. Reading it as a genre risks flattening Alice Coltrane's Vedantic practice, Sanders' Islam and the Detroit collectives' Black nationalism into one aesthetic mood.

genres.name: Loft Jazz

origin.city: New York (SoHo / NoHo / Lower East Side)

genres.oneLine: The second generation of the avant-garde, playing in their own apartments because no club would book them.
genres.summary: By the early 1970s the New York jazz club economy had collapsed for anyone playing anything challenging, and Manhattan was full of cheap industrial loft space. Musicians rented lofts, lived in them, and put on concerts in them. Sam Rivers and Beatrice Rivers ran Studio Rivbea on Bond Street from 1970 until around 1980; Rashied Ali ran Ali's Alley; there was also Environ, the Ladies' Fort and Studio We. What resulted was less a style than a scene with a shared condition: no owner taking a cut, no set length, no drinks minimum, an audience that came specifically for this. The music sat between free jazz and composition — the AACM and BAG diaspora had arrived from Chicago and St. Louis, and their compositional discipline mixed with New York energy playing. Duos and unusual small formats flourished because they were cheap. The five-LP Wildflowers set, recorded at Studio Rivbea over ten days in May 1976, is the scene's document. Gentrification ended it: the same loft space that had been affordable in 1972 was not by 1982.

musicalTraits.harmony: Wide open — freely atonal, modal, and occasionally straightforwardly tonal within one set. No single harmonic system.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Free time predominates, but the second generation reintroduced grooves, ostinatos and explicit metric structures more readily than the 1960s players.
musicalTraits.form: Composed frames around free sections. Duo and trio formats where structure has to be negotiated live.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Saxophone-heavy, with the all-saxophone ensemble emerging here. Cello, tuba, bass clarinet and multiple percussionists are common.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Collective, long-form and highly interactive, typically in small groups where every player is audible at all times.
musicalTraits.timbre: Dry, close, unglamorous — most of these recordings were made in the rooms themselves, and the acoustics are part of the document.

earMarkers: Recordings that sound like a room, not a studio — you can hear the space and the audience
Unusual small line-ups: two saxophones and nothing else, or saxophone and drums alone
Written composed sections bracketing long free improvisations
Grooves and repeated figures returning, which 1960s free jazz mostly avoided
Sets that clearly ran as long as the musicians wanted

keyFigures.name: Sam Rivers
keyFigures.instrument: tenor and soprano saxophone, flute, piano
keyFigures.why: Ran Studio Rivbea, the scene's centre, and played long-form free music with unusual structural clarity.

keyFigures.name: David Murray
keyFigures.why: Arrived from California as a very young man and became the scene's most prolific figure; his tone reaches back to Ayler and Hawkins at once.

keyFigures.name: Julius Hemphill
keyFigures.why: Brought BAG's compositional approach from St. Louis and formed the World Saxophone Quartet out of the scene.

keyFigures.name: Anthony Braxton
keyFigures.why: A constant presence, bringing AACM structural thinking into the New York environment.

keyFigures.name: Rashied Ali
keyFigures.why: Coltrane's last drummer, who ran Ali's Alley and issued the scene's records on his own Survival label.

keyFigures.name: Oliver Lake
keyFigures.why: BAG co-founder and WSQ member; among the scene's most consistent composer-bandleaders.

genres.contested: Whether loft jazz is a style or a real-estate situation. Critics at the time used it as a catch-all for New York avant-garde music in the 1970s, and the musicians involved played very differently from each other. This guide treats it as a scene-genre — defined by its conditions of production, which genuinely shaped the music that came out.

genres.name: Jazz Fusion
genres.oneLine: Jazz plugged into amplifiers and rebuilt around rock volume and funk rhythm, with the improvising kept intact.
genres.summary: Two things happen at once around 1969. Jazz musicians start using electric instruments — Fender Rhodes, electric bass, distorted guitar, ring modulators — and they stop swinging, replacing the triplet lilt with straight-eighth rock and funk feels. Miles Davis is the hinge: In a Silent Way in 1969 is quiet and static, Bitches Brew in 1970 is dense and assembled in the edit room by Teo Macero, and by 1972 On the Corner is an unbroken funk machine. Nearly everyone in those bands then formed their own: Weather Report, Mahavishnu Orchestra, Return to Forever, Headhunters, Lifetime. The results were technically formidable and often extremely popular, which is why the backlash was severe — critics called it a commercial capitulation and the neo-bop movement in the 1980s defined itself against it. The music itself varies enormously: Mahavishnu is aggressive odd-meter virtuosity, Weather Report is collective and textural, Headhunters is groove-first. What they share is electricity, straight eighths, and the assumption that a rock audience's volume and energy could be jazz's too.

musicalTraits.harmony: Modal vamps and pedal points dominate, with slash chords, suspended voicings, and stretches where harmony is essentially static.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Straight eighths from rock and funk, plus odd meters — 7/8, 9/8, 5/4 — as a virtuosic marker in the Mahavishnu and Return to Forever wing.
musicalTraits.form: Long, sectional, often built from vamps rather than song forms. Studio editing becomes a compositional tool.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Fender Rhodes and synthesizers, electric bass, distorted electric guitar, expanded percussion. Horns often processed with wah or echo.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Modal and pentatonic soloing at rock volume, with electric guitar and synthesizer as lead voices alongside horns.
musicalTraits.timbre: Effects as composition — wah, ring modulation, fuzz, echo, and the Rhodes' bell-like decay. Studio production is part of the music.

earMarkers: Electric piano (Fender Rhodes) instead of acoustic — bell-like and slightly bent
Straight, even eighth notes with a rock or funk feel, no swing
Distorted electric guitar taking solos where a saxophone would have
Bars that don't come out in fours — count and you'll lose your place
Long stretches on one chord with the intensity coming from rhythm and volume

keyFigures.name: Miles Davis
keyFigures.why: Made the transition audible across four years and staffed most of the bands that followed.

keyFigures.name: Joe Zawinul
keyFigures.why: Weather Report's principal writer and an early master of the synthesizer as an orchestral rather than a novelty instrument.

keyFigures.name: Wayne Shorter
keyFigures.why: Weather Report's other half; brought post-bop compositional ambiguity into an electric setting.

keyFigures.name: John McLaughlin
keyFigures.why: Mahavishnu Orchestra defined the high-velocity, odd-meter, Indian-influenced wing of fusion.

keyFigures.name: Herbie Hancock
keyFigures.why: Head Hunters in 1973 took fusion into a funk-first direction and became one of the best-selling jazz records ever made.

keyFigures.name: Jaco Pastorius
keyFigures.why: Redefined the fretless electric bass as a lead melodic instrument with a singing, harmonics-rich tone.

keyFigures.name: Tony Williams
keyFigures.why: Lifetime, formed in 1969, was arguably louder and more rock-committed than anything Miles did.

genres.contested: Whether fusion is a genre or a period. 'Jazz-rock' and 'fusion' are used interchangeably by some and distinguished by others (jazz-rock for the 1969–74 aggressive wing, fusion for what came after). The critical rehabilitation of the era is recent and still contested; a lot of writers still treat 1975–85 fusion as a lost decade.

genres.name: Jazz-Funk
genres.oneLine: The groove is the composition — jazz players building on a bass line and a drum break instead of a chord sequence.
genres.summary: Fusion took jazz toward rock; jazz-funk took it toward James Brown and Sly Stone. The difference is priority: in fusion the solo is usually the point and the groove supports it, while in jazz-funk the groove is the piece and the solo is one layer in it. The rhythm is on the one, with a syncopated electric bass line as the primary compositional material, clavinet or Rhodes stabs, a horn section playing tight riffs, and drum parts built for dancing. Herbie Hancock's Head Hunters, Donald Byrd's work with the Mizell brothers, Roy Ayers' Ubiquity, Lonnie Liston Smith and the whole CTI catalogue mark the range from serious to slick. It was commercially the most successful jazz of the 1970s and, for that reason, the most despised by critics of the period. Its afterlife is disproportionate: hip-hop producers mined these records so thoroughly that a huge share of the sampled jazz in rap comes from a narrow band of 1969–79 jazz-funk, which then fed acid jazz, jazz rap and the whole Brainfeeder orbit.

musicalTraits.harmony: Vamp-based — usually one or two chords, often minor seventh or dominant with a raised ninth, sustained for the whole track.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Sixteenth-note funk with the accent on the one. Syncopated bass lines and drum patterns designed to be looped, whether or not anyone intended that.
musicalTraits.form: Groove, horn riff, solos over the groove, breakdown, out. Song forms in the vocal material; open vamps otherwise.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Electric bass, clavinet, Rhodes, ARP and Moog synths, wah guitar, horn section, congas alongside the kit.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Present but rationed and blues-pentatonic in orientation. Nobody is running changes.
musicalTraits.timbre: Warm analogue production, heavy compression on the drums, synth bass and clavinet as textural signatures.

earMarkers: A bass line you'd recognise on its own — it is the tune
Clavinet or wah guitar chopping out sixteenth notes
The whole band hitting hard on beat one and leaving space after it
Horn riffs that repeat as a hook rather than developing
Drum breaks where everything drops out except the kit — later sampled to death

keyFigures.name: Herbie Hancock
keyFigures.why: Head Hunters put a jazz musician's harmonic mind inside a Sly Stone rhythm section and sold enormously.

keyFigures.name: Donald Byrd
keyFigures.why: His Mizell brothers records are the most fully realised jazz-funk productions and the most sampled.

keyFigures.name: Roy Ayers
keyFigures.why: Made vibraphone-led jazz-funk with a songwriting sensibility; sampled more than almost anyone in the idiom.

keyFigures.name: Lonnie Liston Smith
keyFigures.why: Connected the spiritual jazz wing to the dancefloor with a floating, echo-heavy sound.

keyFigures.name: Eddie Harris
keyFigures.why: Early adopter of the electrified saxophone and a genuine funk writer, not a jazz musician visiting.

keyFigures.name: Grover Washington Jr.
keyFigures.why: The commercial bridge from jazz-funk into smooth jazz, and a much better player than that lineage suggests.

genres.contested: The boundary with fusion, which is a matter of emphasis rather than kind. Also whether the 1990s 'rare groove' reissue framing — which selected records for danceability and sample potential — has distorted which artists are remembered.

genres.name: Free Funk & Harmolodics
genres.oneLine: Free jazz over a hard funk backbeat, with everybody playing a lead line at once.
genres.summary: In 1975 Ornette Coleman plugged in. Prime Time paired two electric guitars, two electric basses and two drummers with his alto, playing his harmolodic theory in an idiom built on funk backbeats. Harmolodics is Coleman's own concept and he explained it inconsistently, but the working version is: harmony, movement and melody have equal status, no instrument is subordinate, and players can transpose a line to whatever register or key suits their instrument while it remains 'the same' line. In practice that produces a thick, deliberately unresolved texture where four or five people are all playing melody over a groove that stays put. Ronald Shannon Jackson's Decoding Society and James Blood Ulmer took it in harder, more rock-facing directions, and it became a direct input to the downtown New York scene and to the whole idea that free improvisation could coexist with a heavy beat. Coleman's own Prime Time records remain the clearest statement, and Song X with Pat Metheny in 1985 dragged the approach onto a much larger stage.

musicalTraits.harmony: Harmolodic — no fixed key centre, instruments playing lines in different keys simultaneously, consonance and dissonance treated as equally usable.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Hard funk and second-line backbeats, often with two drummers producing overlapping rather than unified patterns.
musicalTraits.form: Themes stated in unison then abandoned; the groove continues while the melodic content roams free.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Doubled everything — two guitars, two basses, two drummers — plus alto saxophone or trumpet on top.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Simultaneous and non-hierarchical. There is often no soloist because everyone is soloing.
musicalTraits.timbre: Bright, trebly, deliberately cluttered. Guitars are clean-toned and busy rather than distorted and sustaining.

earMarkers: A rock-solid funk beat underneath music that is otherwise completely unresolved
Two guitars and two basses all playing different lines at once
Melodies that sound simple and singable, dropped into total harmonic chaos
No obvious soloist — several people appear to be leading simultaneously
Everything sounding slightly out of tune with everything else, on purpose

keyFigures.name: Ornette Coleman
keyFigures.why: Invented harmolodics and Prime Time; the entire idiom is his theory made audible.

keyFigures.name: Ronald Shannon Jackson
keyFigures.why: The Decoding Society took harmolodic principles into denser, more composed and harder-hitting territory.

keyFigures.name: James Blood Ulmer
keyFigures.why: Applied harmolodics to blues and rock forms; his guitar tuning and attack have no real precedent.

keyFigures.name: Jamaaladeen Tacuma
keyFigures.why: Prime Time's bassist, who treated the bass as a lead melodic voice rather than a foundation.

keyFigures.name: Bern Nix
keyFigures.why: Prime Time's clean-toned guitarist, whose refusal to play rock guitar clichés is central to the band's sound.

genres.contested: Whether harmolodics is a coherent theory or an idiosyncratic vocabulary. Coleman's explanations varied and musicians who played the music describe it in incompatible ways. This guide treats free funk as a genre and harmolodics as one leader's method for producing it — which is an interpretive choice, not a settled position.

genres.name: Smooth Jazz
genres.oneLine: Jazz-funk sanded down for radio: melody in front, solos short, nothing that would make a listener flinch.
genres.summary: Smooth jazz is a radio format that became a genre, and it should be described that way rather than sneered at. Its ancestry is real — Grover Washington Jr., Wes Montgomery's late CTI records, Bob James, the Crusaders — and its ingredients are consistent: a strong singable melody carried by soprano saxophone or guitar, a mid-tempo funk or quiet-storm groove, glossy production with a lot of reverb, and improvisation kept short and consonant. Kenny G's Breathless in 1992 sold in the millions and became the reference point for everything wrong with the format for jazz critics, which is a lot of weight to put on one record. The format's radio dominance from the late 1980s through the early 2000s meant that for a large number of people this was what 'jazz' meant, which is part of why the hostility was so intense. Musically the interesting question is what got removed: harmonic risk, rhythmic disruption, and the possibility that a solo might fail. Nothing is at stake, deliberately. Some of the players — Washington, Larry Carlton, Lee Ritenour — could do far more than the format asked.

musicalTraits.harmony: Consonant and stable — major sevenths, gentle ii–V motion, no altered dominants. Modulations are for lift, not tension.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Mid-tempo funk, quiet-storm ballad feels, and later programmed drums and quantised grids.
musicalTraits.form: Pop song form. Melody, short solo, melody, fade. Tracks run to radio length.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Soprano and alto saxophone, clean electric guitar, synthesizers and DX7-era electric pianos, fretless bass, programmed and live drums.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Brief and melodic, staying inside the harmony. Solos are usually written or worked out in advance.
musicalTraits.timbre: Highly produced — chorus, digital reverb, gated drums. The 1980s studio sound is inseparable from the genre.

earMarkers: A soprano saxophone playing a melody you could hum after one listen
Everything mixed clean, wide and glossy, with a lot of reverb
Solos that last eight bars and never go outside the chord
A steady mid-tempo groove that stays exactly the same throughout
Tracks that end in a fade at about four and a half minutes

keyFigures.name: Grover Washington Jr.
keyFigures.why: The genuine link between jazz-funk and the format; a serious improviser whose commercial records set the template.

keyFigures.name: Bob James
keyFigures.why: CTI arranger whose 1970s records supplied both the format's sound and a great many hip-hop samples.

keyFigures.name: David Sanborn
keyFigures.why: His piercing, blues-derived alto tone became the most imitated sound in the idiom, though his own playing has more bite than the copies.

keyFigures.name: Kenny G
keyFigures.why: The best-selling instrumentalist of the era and the lightning rod for every argument about the format's legitimacy.

keyFigures.name: The Crusaders
keyFigures.why: Went from hard bop as the Jazz Crusaders to a groove-based crossover sound that prefigured the whole format.

genres.contested: Whether it counts as jazz. The critical consensus has been dismissive for forty years, and the argument that it removes improvisational risk has force. The counter-argument is that dismissing it wholesale erases the Black radio and quiet-storm context it grew out of, and flattens genuine players into one caricature. This guide includes it as a real branch with a real lineage, and does not pretend to be neutral about the ceiling.

genres.name: Acid Jazz
genres.oneLine: DJs rediscovering 1970s jazz-funk on the dancefloor, then hiring bands to play new music that sounded like it.
genres.summary: This one starts with record collecting, not with musicians. London club DJs in the mid-1980s — Gilles Peterson and Chris Bangs among them — were playing forgotten 1960s and 70s jazz-funk, soul jazz and Latin records to dancers, and the name 'acid jazz' began as a joke on acid house. From there it went two ways: reissues and compilations that resurrected a whole layer of neglected recordings, and new bands playing original material in that idiom — Brand New Heavies, Incognito, Jamiroquai, the James Taylor Quartet, Galliano — often with hip-hop production techniques, live rhythm sections and rap or soul vocals over the top. The Acid Jazz label was founded in 1987 by Peterson and Eddie Piller; Peterson later left to start Talkin' Loud. Musically it is more a curatorial position than a technique: the groove and the crate-digger's ear are the constants. Its importance is downstream — it built the UK infrastructure of clubs, labels and radio that later produced broken beat, the 2010s London jazz scene, and much of the audience for both.

musicalTraits.harmony: Borrowed wholesale from soul jazz and jazz-funk — modal vamps, minor sevenths, gospel cadences. Rarely harmonically ambitious on its own terms.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Danceable funk and boogaloo at club tempos, later incorporating breakbeats and programmed drums alongside live players.
musicalTraits.form: Song and groove structures built for DJ use — long intros, breakdowns, clean beat-matchable sections.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Hammond organ, Rhodes, electric bass, horn section, turntables and samplers, plus soul and rap vocals.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Short and functional. The idiom is about feel, not solo development.
musicalTraits.timbre: Deliberately retro — analogue keyboards, warm bass, drum sounds modelled on 1970s records even when programmed.

earMarkers: Hammond organ and horn riffs that sound like 1971 but were recorded in 1993
A rock-steady club tempo designed for a DJ to mix in and out of
Rapping or soul singing over what is otherwise a jazz-funk band
Sampled drum breaks sitting alongside a live rhythm section
Very short solos, if any

keyFigures.name: Gilles Peterson
keyFigures.why: Co-named the movement, co-founded Acid Jazz then Talkin' Loud, and has kept building the UK's jazz infrastructure ever since.

keyFigures.name: Brand New Heavies
keyFigures.why: The most successful of the live acid jazz bands and the closest to a functioning 1970s jazz-funk group.

keyFigures.name: Incognito
keyFigures.why: Jean-Paul 'Bluey' Maunick's group provided the idiom's most durable songwriting.

keyFigures.name: James Taylor Quartet
keyFigures.why: Hammond-driven and closest to the soul jazz source material, minus the improvisation.

keyFigures.name: Roy Ayers
keyFigures.why: The most important living ancestor, adopted by the scene and actively recording with it.

genres.contested: Whether it is a genre or a DJ marketing category. Musicians in it frequently rejected the label. It also has an uneasy relationship with the music it revived — the acid jazz audience discovered soul jazz and jazz-funk via compilations that often stripped the original context away.

genres.name: Jazz Rap
genres.oneLine: Hip-hop producers building beats from jazz records, and then jazz musicians answering back.
genres.summary: It starts with sampling. Producers in the late 1980s went looking for breaks in their parents' jazz collections and found that upright bass, Rhodes and horn stabs sat beautifully under rapping. A Tribe Called Quest's The Low End Theory in 1991 is the pivot: sparse, bass-forward, built on jazz samples, with Ron Carter playing upright bass on one track. Gang Starr, Digable Planets, Pete Rock, Us3 and the Native Tongues collective make up the rest of the first wave. Then it goes both ways. Guru's Jazzmatazz in 1993 put live jazz musicians in the studio with a rapper; Miles Davis's last album, Doo-Bop, was a hip-hop collaboration; Branford Marsalis's Buckshot LeFonque and Steve Coleman's projects came from the jazz side. The lasting influence is rhythmic: the boom-bap feel — a heavy, slightly-behind, sampled-sounding backbeat — became a legitimate jazz groove, and by the 2010s drummers like Chris Dave, Karriem Riggins and Marcus Gilmore had absorbed it as a first language. That is the line running into the LA beat scene and the London revival.

musicalTraits.harmony: Sample-derived. Loops of jazz records supply the harmony wholesale, often two or four bars repeated with no development.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Boom-bap — a hard, slightly loose backbeat around 85–95 BPM, with swung sixteenths and deliberate timing imperfections.
musicalTraits.form: Verse–chorus rap structure over looped material, with the loop as the harmonic and formal constant.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Sampler and turntables first; upright bass, Rhodes, saxophone and trumpet added live in the second wave.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Initially the rapping is the improvisation-descended element. Live solos appear from Jazzmatazz onward.
musicalTraits.timbre: Warm, dusty, filtered — the sound of vinyl sampled at low bit rates is an aesthetic choice, not a limitation.

earMarkers: A short loop of an old jazz record repeating under the whole track
Upright bass, which almost no other hip-hop uses
A drum feel that's slightly behind and slightly loose rather than machine-tight
Muted trumpet or Rhodes chords used as a hook
Vinyl crackle and filtering left audible in the mix

keyFigures.name: A Tribe Called Quest
keyFigures.why: The Low End Theory established the sparse, bass-forward jazz-sample aesthetic that everything else worked from.

keyFigures.name: Guru
keyFigures.why: Gang Starr's rapper and the Jazzmatazz series' architect — the first sustained attempt to put rappers and live jazz players in one room.

keyFigures.name: DJ Premier
keyFigures.why: Gang Starr's producer and the definitive boom-bap sound designer; his chopping technique is a compositional method.

keyFigures.name: Pete Rock
keyFigures.why: Built the lushest horn-sample production of the era, working from soul jazz and hard bop records.

keyFigures.name: Digable Planets
keyFigures.why: Took the aesthetic furthest into explicit jazz reference, right down to the bebop-cool persona.

keyFigures.name: J Dilla
keyFigures.why: His deliberately unquantised drum programming changed how a generation of jazz drummers thinks about time.

genres.contested: Whether it belongs in a jazz lineage or a hip-hop one. It is unambiguously hip-hop as music; its inclusion here is on the grounds of what it sent back — the boom-bap feel is now standard jazz drumming vocabulary. Filing it as a jazz genre risks the old habit of claiming Black popular music for jazz whenever it becomes respectable.

genres.name: Nu Jazz & Electronic Jazz
genres.oneLine: Jazz improvisation over programmed electronic rhythm — the drum machine as bandmate rather than backing track.
genres.summary: Where acid jazz revived old records and jazz rap sampled them, nu jazz starts from electronic dance music and adds improvisers. The rhythmic base is drum and bass, house, broken beat or downtempo — programmed, quantised or deliberately un-quantised — and horns, keyboards and bass improvise across it. There were several parallel scenes. In Norway, Bugge Wesseltoft's New Conception of Jazz and Nils Petter Molvær's Khmer in 1997 put ECM-style trumpet lyricism over dub and electronica, and Jaga Jazzist built a large band around programming. In London, the broken beat scene around West London and labels like Talkin' Loud extended acid jazz's clubbing into more complex rhythmic territory. In Germany, Jazzanova and the Compost/Sonar Kollektiv orbit did it as production. St Germain in Paris put house beats under blues and jazz samples and sold two million records. The best of it treats the beat as a partner — something to play against — and the weakest of it is a lounge compilation. Its influence runs directly into the current London scene.

musicalTraits.harmony: Modal and vamp-based, with a strong debt to ECM's floating consonance and to house music's static two-chord loops.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Programmed — drum and bass at 170 BPM, house at 125, broken beat's displaced syncopations, downtempo at 90. Live drums often play with or against the grid.
musicalTraits.form: Track-based rather than song-based: build, drop, breakdown. Solos happen inside a producer's arrangement.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Laptop, sampler and drum machine alongside trumpet, saxophone, Rhodes and double or electric bass.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Real but constrained. The soloist works over a fixed grid and a fixed harmony, closer to a dub toaster's role than a bebop soloist's.
musicalTraits.timbre: Processed heavily — delay and reverb on horns, filtered pads, sub-bass. Molvær's echo-drenched trumpet is the signature sound.

earMarkers: Programmed drums that are clearly electronic sitting under acoustic solos
Trumpet or saxophone soaked in delay and reverb, played sparsely
Deep sub-bass that no acoustic instrument could produce
A track that builds and drops like dance music rather than stating a head
Harmony that barely moves across five or six minutes

keyFigures.name: Nils Petter Molvær
keyFigures.why: Khmer in 1997 defined the ECM-meets-electronica sound and remains the idiom's clearest statement.

keyFigures.name: Bugge Wesseltoft
keyFigures.why: New Conception of Jazz and the Jazzland label built the Norwegian scene as an ongoing project.

keyFigures.name: Jazzanova
keyFigures.why: The Berlin production team that connected broken beat, Brazilian material and jazz into a coherent European sound.

keyFigures.name: St Germain
keyFigures.why: Ludovic Navarre's Tourist sold to an audience far outside jazz and proved the format could carry a mass market.

keyFigures.name: Jaga Jazzist
keyFigures.why: A large Norwegian ensemble writing for horns, strings and electronics as one machine.

keyFigures.name: Cinematic Orchestra
keyFigures.why: Jason Swinscoe's group moved from sample-based production to a fully live ensemble without changing the aesthetic.

genres.contested: The name. 'Nu jazz' was largely a retail category and few of the musicians used it. It has also been criticised as jazz's least improvisational branch, where the improviser is a texture inside someone else's production. Both charges are fair for a lot of the catalogue and unfair for the best of it.

genres.name: LA Beat-Scene Jazz
genres.oneLine: Jazz musicians who grew up on J Dilla and Flying Lotus, playing with a producer's ear and a beatmaker's sense of time.
genres.summary: Two Los Angeles streams converged. One was the beat scene around Low End Theory, the club night that ran from 2006, and Flying Lotus's Brainfeeder label — instrumental hip-hop built on sample manipulation, sub-bass and deliberately wonky, off-grid timing inherited from J Dilla. The other was the West Coast Get Down, a group of musicians who had come up together in Los Angeles schools and played together for a decade before anyone noticed: Kamasi Washington, Thundercat, Terrace Martin, Ronald Bruner Jr., Cameron Graves, Miles Mosley. Thundercat is the physical link, playing bass on Brainfeeder records and in jazz contexts simultaneously. Kendrick Lamar's To Pimp a Butterfly in 2015 put nearly all of them on a mainstream rap record; Washington's three-hour The Epic the same year presented the jazz side with choir, strings and unembarrassed spiritual-jazz ambition. The music combines Coltrane-quartet modal intensity, 1970s spiritual jazz orchestration, and rhythm sections that think in terms of feel and pocket rather than swing.

musicalTraits.harmony: Modal and pentatonic, McCoy Tyner-derived, over pedal points, with gospel and soul progressions and lush orchestral or choral layering.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Dilla-descended: deliberately off-grid, with the snare pushed or dragged so the beat feels drunk but stays locked. Hip-hop tempos alongside fast swing.
musicalTraits.form: Long-form and suite-like on the jazz side; loop-and-transform on the beat side. Both prefer accumulation to development.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Six-string electric bass, synthesizers, saxophone, keys, two drummers on occasion, plus choir and strings.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Extended and intensity-driven, closer to spiritual jazz than to post-bop. Solos are long and go for transcendence rather than cleverness.
musicalTraits.timbre: Producer-shaped: heavy sub-bass, saturated synths, vocal layering, and a mix aesthetic drawn from hip-hop rather than jazz engineering.

earMarkers: A beat that sounds slightly drunk — snare landing late — but never actually loses time
Sub-bass and synthesizers sitting under acoustic saxophone and drums
Choir or massed vocals used as an orchestral section
Long modal solos that build toward ecstasy in the Coltrane manner
Production values from hip-hop: everything loud, wide and compressed

keyFigures.name: Kamasi Washington
keyFigures.why: The Epic put large-scale spiritual jazz in front of an audience that had not been listening to jazz.

keyFigures.name: Thundercat
keyFigures.why: The scene's connective tissue, moving between Brainfeeder, Kendrick Lamar and jazz contexts as one practice.

keyFigures.name: Flying Lotus
keyFigures.why: Founded Brainfeeder and built the beat aesthetic; also Alice Coltrane's great-nephew, which is not incidental to the music.

keyFigures.name: Terrace Martin
keyFigures.why: The producer-musician who brokered the jazz players onto To Pimp a Butterfly.

keyFigures.name: Robert Glasper
keyFigures.why: Not LA-based, but Black Radio in 2012 established the template of jazz pianist as R&B and hip-hop bandleader.

keyFigures.name: Chris Dave
keyFigures.why: The drummer who most fully translated Dilla's programmed feel back onto an acoustic kit.

genres.contested: Whether it is a genre or a network. Kamasi Washington's large-ensemble spiritual jazz and Flying Lotus's electronic production have little in common technically; what links them is a city, a label, and a set of collaborations. Some critics argue the 'jazz renaissance' framing around 2015 oversold a scene that had been working for a decade already.

genres.name: ECM & Nordic Chamber Jazz
genres.oneLine: Jazz built around space, silence and sustained sound — recorded so precisely the room becomes an instrument.
genres.summary: Manfred Eicher founded ECM in Munich in 1969 and produced almost everything on it himself, with engineer Jan Erik Kongshaug at Talent Studio in Oslo for a large part of the catalogue. The recording aesthetic — long natural reverb, extreme dynamic range, every instrument separated and audible, piano and cymbals given room to decay — is so consistent that it constitutes a compositional element, and the phrase 'the most beautiful sound next to silence' came from a review and stuck as the label's own slogan. Musically the identifying features are slow harmonic rhythm, folk-derived melody, restraint, and a relationship to European classical music that is unembarrassed rather than programmatic. Jan Garbarek's saxophone tone — cold, pure, enormous — became the sound people mean by 'Nordic'. Keith Jarrett's solo concerts, especially Köln in 1975, made the label commercially significant. It is contested whether this is a genre or a producer's taste, and the argument is real: ECM also released Art Ensemble of Chicago, Steve Reich and Meredith Monk. But the Nordic chamber wing is coherent enough to name.

musicalTraits.harmony: Slow-moving, modal, often built on suspended and open voicings that avoid clear resolution. Folk modes from Scandinavian and Eastern European sources.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Rubato and free-time passages alongside straight eighths; swing appears rarely. Drummers play colour and texture as much as pulse.
musicalTraits.form: Long, patient, often through-composed. Pieces develop by accumulation and change of density rather than by chorus structure.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Piano, saxophone, double bass, drums, but also guitar, oud, tabla, string quartet and voice; unusual pairings are routine.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Restrained and thematic. Melodic development matters more than harmonic navigation or rhythmic display.
musicalTraits.timbre: The defining parameter. Long natural reverb, wide dynamics, the decay of notes treated as content.

earMarkers: Enormous natural-sounding reverb — the room is clearly part of the record
Very quiet passages that demand you turn it up, then sudden fullness
Melodies that sound like folk songs rather than jazz heads
Drums played with mallets and cymbals left to ring out
Almost no swing feel, and often no steady pulse at all

keyFigures.name: Manfred Eicher
keyFigures.why: Produced the overwhelming majority of the catalogue; the label's aesthetic is a single person's editorial ear applied for fifty years.

keyFigures.name: Jan Garbarek
keyFigures.why: His tone and his use of Norwegian folk material define what 'Nordic jazz' means to most listeners.

keyFigures.name: Keith Jarrett
keyFigures.why: The solo concerts made improvised piano a concert-hall event and gave ECM a commercial base.

keyFigures.name: Eberhard Weber
keyFigures.why: Built an entirely personal instrument and a body of chamber-jazz writing around it.

keyFigures.name: Terje Rypdal
keyFigures.why: Brought sustained, distorted, orchestral electric guitar into the label's otherwise acoustic world.

keyFigures.name: Tomasz Stańko
keyFigures.why: The Polish wing — darker, more Miles-derived, and connected to a Central European free-jazz history the Nordic players did not share.

genres.contested: Whether 'ECM jazz' names a genre or a label's house taste. The catalogue includes free jazz, contemporary classical, Renaissance music and Art Ensemble of Chicago records, which no stylistic definition covers. This guide names the Nordic chamber wing specifically and treats the label as its institutional home rather than as a synonym. There is also a persistent criticism that the aesthetic prizes surface beauty over risk.

genres.name: Neo-Bop & the Young Lions
genres.oneLine: A deliberate return to acoustic hard bop and swing, made by conservatory-trained players who thought fusion had been a wrong turn.
genres.summary: Wynton Marsalis signed to Columbia in 1981 at nineteen, won Grammys in both jazz and classical categories in 1983, and became the public face of an argument: that jazz had a tradition, that the tradition was acoustic and blues-based and ran from New Orleans through Ellington and Parker to the mid-1960s, and that fusion and free jazz had taken the music away from it. The music that followed is technically formidable and largely acoustic — quintets and sextets, standards and originals in a post-bop language, sharp suits, no synthesizers. It coincided with the institutionalisation of jazz: university programmes, Jazz at Lincoln Center from 1987 with Marsalis as artistic director, the Ken Burns documentary in 2001, repertory orchestras, NEA Jazz Masters. The criticism, made forcefully by Nicholas Payton, Greg Osby and others, is that this froze the music into a museum canon at exactly the moment it should have been moving. The defence is that a generation of musicians got a rigorous grounding they would not otherwise have had. Both are true and the argument has not settled.

musicalTraits.harmony: Bebop and post-bop harmony played with conservatory precision — full changes, extended forms, and a deliberate refusal of modal shortcuts.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Acoustic swing restored as the default, with New Orleans second-line and Latin feels used as compositional colour.
musicalTraits.form: Standards and originals in traditional forms, plus extended suites, especially in Marsalis's later large-scale works.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Acoustic quintet and sextet, big band, no electric instruments as a matter of policy in the strict wing.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Highly schooled, harmonically precise, and consciously in dialogue with recorded history — quotation and stylistic allusion are common.
musicalTraits.timbre: Warm, controlled, well-recorded acoustic sound. Digital-era production without digital-era instruments.

earMarkers: Entirely acoustic instruments, with a swing feel front and centre
Playing that is audibly virtuosic and audibly schooled
Deliberate references to earlier styles — a New Orleans strut, an Ellington voicing
Standards played straight rather than deconstructed
A clean, warm, modern recording of a determinedly old-fashioned band

keyFigures.name: Wynton Marsalis
keyFigures.why: The movement's musician, spokesman and institution-builder; his 1997 Pulitzer for Blood on the Fields was the first awarded to a jazz work.

keyFigures.name: Branford Marsalis
keyFigures.why: Took the same training in a looser direction, including work with Sting and a hip-hop project his brother would not have made.

keyFigures.name: Terence Blanchard
keyFigures.why: Came through the Jazz Messengers, then built a major second career in film scoring and opera.

keyFigures.name: Joshua Redman
keyFigures.why: Won the Monk competition in 1991 and became the most visible of the second Young Lions wave.

keyFigures.name: Roy Hargrove
keyFigures.why: The one who most obviously refused the boundaries — hard bop, Afro-Cuban, and the RH Factor's neo-soul, all seriously.

keyFigures.name: Marcus Roberts
keyFigures.why: Went furthest back, rebuilding stride and ragtime technique inside a modern practice.

genres.contested: This genre is an argument as much as a style. Critics including Nicholas Payton and Greg Osby have argued it produced a canon-policing orthodoxy that damaged the music's forward motion and marginalised the avant-garde. Defenders point to the training, the archives and the institutions that resulted. The dispute over who gets to define the tradition is the actual content of the category.

genres.name: M-Base
genres.oneLine: Improvisation over interlocking, cyclic rhythmic structures drawn from West African and diasporic music — jazz thinking in loops rather than choruses.
genres.summary: A group of young musicians in Brooklyn in the mid-1980s — Steve Coleman, Greg Osby, Cassandra Wilson, Geri Allen, Robin Eubanks, Graham Haynes, Marvin 'Smitty' Smith — worked out an approach that was neither neo-bop nor free. The rhythmic basis is nested cycles: several repeating patterns of different lengths running simultaneously, so the downbeat is a matter of which layer you follow. That idea comes from West African drumming traditions and their diasporic descendants, and it makes the music feel simultaneously funky and disorienting. Over it, the melodic language is angular, chromatic, and phrased against the grid rather than with it. Coleman coined the acronym, and he has consistently insisted that M-Base names a philosophy of creative growth and shared language rather than a style of music — a distinction most journalism has ignored. That correction matters: the players involved sound quite different from each other, and treating M-Base as a sound rather than a working method misrepresents its own self-description. The influence is enormous and mostly indirect — Vijay Iyer, Steve Lehman, Ambrose Akinmusire and much of what is now called contemporary creative music runs through it.

musicalTraits.harmony: Chromatic and non-functional, often built from symmetrical structures and pitch cells rather than chord progressions.
musicalTraits.rhythm: The centre of the concept. Nested, interlocking cycles of unequal length, odd groupings, and a funk feel that keeps displacing.
musicalTraits.form: Cyclic rather than chorus-based. Sections repeat at different rates and phase against one another.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Alto saxophone, trumpet, trombone, guitar, electric bass, drums; voice used as an instrumental line. Electric and acoustic freely mixed.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Improvising across a shifting grid — the challenge is orientation as much as invention. Collective interaction is expected.
musicalTraits.timbre: Dry, tight, unromantic. Little reverb, hard articulation, and a deliberately unlush ensemble sound.

earMarkers: A groove that is clearly funky but that you cannot easily count
Several repeating patterns of different lengths running at once
Melodic lines that cut across the beat rather than sitting on it
Voice used as another horn, singing wordless lines in unison
A dry, clipped band sound with almost no reverb

keyFigures.name: Steve Coleman
keyFigures.why: Coined the term and has pursued the rhythmic research for forty years, including fieldwork in Ghana, Cuba and India.

keyFigures.name: Greg Osby
keyFigures.why: The other central altoist; later a Blue Note bandleader and a persistent critic of neo-traditionalist orthodoxy.

keyFigures.name: Cassandra Wilson
keyFigures.why: Came out of the collective and then built a singular body of work applying its rhythmic thinking to blues and folk repertoire.

keyFigures.name: Geri Allen
keyFigures.why: Connected M-Base to the AACM lineage and to the mainstream, with a harmonic imagination distinct from anyone else in the group.

keyFigures.name: Robin Eubanks
keyFigures.why: Made the trombone work in a rhythmically demanding idiom that gives it no natural place.

keyFigures.name: Marvin 'Smitty' Smith
keyFigures.why: Executed the interlocking-cycle concept on the kit and made it feel like a groove rather than an exercise.

genres.contested: Whether M-Base is a genre at all. Steve Coleman has stated repeatedly that it is a concept and a way of working, not a style, and that critics who describe an 'M-Base sound' have misunderstood it. This guide includes it as a node because the influence is traceable and the rhythmic approach is identifiable — while noting that the person who named it would object to the framing.

genres.name: Downtown & Punk Jazz
genres.oneLine: Free jazz colliding with hardcore punk, surf, klezmer and cartoon music, usually at high speed and without warning.
genres.summary: Lower Manhattan in the late 1970s and 80s had a scene where the boundary between avant-garde jazz, no wave, punk and contemporary composition simply was not enforced. John Zorn is the organising figure. His game pieces — Cobra above all, from 1984 — are structured improvisations run by a prompter using cue cards, where the rules govern who plays and when but not what. Naked City compressed hardcore punk, film noir soundtracks, country and free jazz into pieces lasting under a minute, switching genre every few seconds. The Lounge Lizards played what Zorn's contemporary John Lurie called 'fake jazz', deadpan and hard-edged. Bill Frisell, Wayne Horvitz, Elliott Sharp, Marc Ribot and Tim Berne all worked across the same rooms — the Knitting Factory from 1987, and before it a network of lofts and galleries. Zorn's Tzadik label from 1995 institutionalised it. The Jewish identity strand — Masada, the Radical Jewish Culture series — brought klezmer modes into an Ornette Coleman quartet format. What holds the scene together is a compositional attitude: rapid juxtaposition, genre as material, and structure imposed on improvisation from outside.

musicalTraits.harmony: Anything, and often several things per minute. Klezmer modes, surf progressions, free atonality and hardcore power chords used as blocks.
musicalTraits.rhythm: Extreme contrast — blast beats next to free time next to a shuffle. Metric stability is a choice, not a default.
musicalTraits.form: Game pieces, file-card compositions, and blocks of material spliced with hard cuts. Duration ranges from 20 seconds to an hour.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Alto saxophone, guitar, bass, drums, plus turntables, samplers, voice, and whatever else. Electric and amplified by default.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Central but governed. The composer sets rules of engagement rather than notes; players improvise inside a designed system.
musicalTraits.timbre: Loud, abrasive, and stylistically promiscuous. Studio and live production are aggressive rather than transparent.

earMarkers: The style changing completely every few seconds without transition
Hardcore punk speed and screaming next to something that swings
Pieces that last thirty seconds and then stop
Klezmer or surf melodies played by a free jazz rhythm section
A group that is clearly following rules you can't hear

keyFigures.name: John Zorn
keyFigures.why: The scene's organiser, composer and label head; the game pieces and Masada are the two poles of his output.

keyFigures.name: Bill Frisell
keyFigures.why: Developed a volume-pedal, delay-heavy Americana-inflected guitar language that was equally at home downtown and on ECM.

keyFigures.name: Marc Ribot
keyFigures.why: The scene's most abrasive and versatile guitarist, moving between Zorn, Tom Waits and Cuban repertoire.

keyFigures.name: Tim Berne
keyFigures.why: Wrote long, intricate compositions for working bands, connecting Julius Hemphill's lineage to the downtown environment.

keyFigures.name: John Lurie
keyFigures.why: The Lounge Lizards' deadpan 'fake jazz' set the scene's tone of ironic seriousness.

keyFigures.name: Elliott Sharp
keyFigures.why: Brought algorithmic and mathematical structures into an otherwise intuitive scene.

genres.contested: Whether it is jazz. A large part of the output has no swing, no blues and no improvisation on changes, and 'downtown' names a geography and a social network rather than a style. Its inclusion here rests on personnel and lineage — most of these players came through free jazz — and on the fact that the scene fed contemporary creative music directly.

genres.name: Contemporary Creative Jazz
genres.oneLine: The current avant-garde mainstream: rhythmically intricate, harmonically dense, conservatory-trained, and drawing on everything at once.
genres.summary: This is where the M-Base rhythmic project, the AACM's compositional discipline, downtown's genre promiscuity and neo-bop's technical training all end up in the same room. The identifying features are rhythmic: odd meters treated as ordinary, metric modulation, polyrhythm as a structural device rather than an effect, and a comfort with hip-hop and electronic feels. Harmonically it draws on spectral and post-tonal composition as readily as on jazz. Vijay Iyer works with rhythmic ratios and cognitive research on rhythm; Steve Lehman applies spectral harmony derived from Tristan Murail; Mary Halvorson has built a guitar language out of pitch-bending and unexpected form; Tyshawn Sorey writes long-form composition that has largely left jazz behind while remaining in dialogue with it; Ambrose Akinmusire, Jason Moran, Craig Taborn, Matana Roberts and Henry Threadgill's later ensembles fill in the range. Institutional support — grants, Pulitzers, MacArthur fellowships, university positions — has replaced the club economy that supported earlier generations, which shapes the music in ways worth noticing: it is composed more and jammed less.

musicalTraits.harmony: Post-tonal, spectral and cluster-based alongside jazz extensions. Harmony is often generated by a system rather than inherited from song form.
musicalTraits.rhythm: The defining domain — metric modulation, nested tuplets, polymeter, and grooves borrowed from hip-hop, West African and South Indian traditions.
musicalTraits.form: Through-composed, modular, or generated by rules. Extended suites and album-length structures are common.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Standard jazz groups plus strings, electronics, laptop processing, and idiosyncratic fixed instrumentations built for a single band.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Deeply integrated with composition — the line between written and improvised is often deliberately hard to hear.
musicalTraits.timbre: Precisely engineered. Electronics and acoustic instruments blended rather than contrasted.

earMarkers: Meters that shift constantly and never settle into four
Written material so intricate it is hard to tell what was improvised
Harmony that sounds like contemporary classical music, not like jazz chords
Hip-hop-derived beats played by an acoustic drummer with total precision
Long album-scale structures rather than a set of tunes

keyFigures.name: Vijay Iyer
keyFigures.why: Combines rhythmic research, M-Base's cyclic thinking and a physical piano attack; also the most articulate writer among the group.

keyFigures.name: Mary Halvorson
keyFigures.why: Built an immediately recognisable guitar vocabulary from pitch-shifting and lurching form, out of Anthony Braxton's tutelage.

keyFigures.name: Tyshawn Sorey
keyFigures.why: Works across improvised music and contemporary composition without treating them as different jobs; won the Pulitzer in 2024.

keyFigures.name: Steve Lehman
keyFigures.why: Imported spectral harmony into an improvising octet, a genuinely new harmonic resource for the music.

keyFigures.name: Jason Moran
keyFigures.why: Connects stride and Fats Waller to hip-hop and conceptual art, often within one piece.

keyFigures.name: Ambrose Akinmusire
keyFigures.why: Writes long-form records about American violence and race with a trumpet language full of cracks and half-valves.

keyFigures.name: Craig Taborn
keyFigures.why: Moves between acoustic trio, solo piano and modular electronics with the same structural mind.

genres.contested: Whether this names anything at all, or is just 'jazz now'. The category is a critics' and grant-committees' convenience for music too composed for neo-bop and too structured for free jazz. Several of the musicians in it reject 'jazz' as a description of their work outright — a position with a long history in this music, from Ellington to Nicholas Payton's #BAM argument.

genres.name: UK Jazz Revival
genres.oneLine: London jazz built on Caribbean, West African and soundsystem rhythm, made by musicians who came up together and play for dancers.
genres.summary: The most striking thing about the current London scene is the rhythm, and where it comes from. These musicians grew up with grime, jungle, Afrobeats, dub, calypso and broken beat as native languages, and the jazz they make is organised around those feels rather than around swing. Sons of Kemet built a band from tuba, two drummers and Shabaka Hutchings' saxophone, playing what amounts to a Caribbean carnival band's rhythmic logic. Ezra Collective run Afrobeat and reggae under jazz soloing. Nubya Garcia, Moses Boyd, Theon Cross, Emma-Jean Thackray and Yussef Dayes fill out the range. The infrastructure is as important as the music: Tomorrow's Warriors, the free youth programme co-founded in 1991 by bassist Gary Crosby and Janine Irons, trained a large proportion of the scene and did so with an explicit commitment to reaching Black and female musicians who the conservatory route was not reaching. Gilles Peterson's Brownswood released the We Out Here compilation in 2018, which is when the rest of the world noticed. The audience is young, and it dances, which has not been true of jazz in Britain for a very long time.

musicalTraits.harmony: Modal, vamp-based and often minor-key, with spiritual jazz's pedal points and Afrobeat's two-chord frames. Harmonic complexity is not the priority.
musicalTraits.rhythm: The centre of everything: Afrobeat, dub, jungle, grime, calypso and second-line feels, frequently with two drummers or a drummer plus percussion.
musicalTraits.form: Groove-driven and often long, with slow-building structures aimed at a live, standing audience rather than a seated one.
musicalTraits.instrumentation: Tuba as a bass instrument, tenor and soprano saxophone, keys, twin drum kits, electronics, and MCs or singers as guests.
musicalTraits.improvisation: Present and extended, but subordinate to the groove — solos build collective intensity rather than displaying harmonic navigation.
musicalTraits.timbre: Soundsystem-informed: heavy low end, dub-style delay and reverb, and mixes made for large speakers.

earMarkers: Tuba playing the bass line instead of a double bass or electric bass
Two drummers, playing complementary rather than identical patterns
Grooves that come from Afrobeat, dub or jungle rather than from swing
Dub-style echo thrown across horns and drums
Music clearly made for a crowd that is standing up

keyFigures.name: Shabaka Hutchings
keyFigures.why: The scene's most visible figure, running Sons of Kemet, The Comet Is Coming and Shabaka and the Ancestors simultaneously, then abandoning the saxophone for flutes in 2023.

keyFigures.name: Nubya Garcia
keyFigures.why: The clearest link back to spiritual jazz and to Caribbean rhythm, with a big, unhurried tone.

keyFigures.name: Moses Boyd
keyFigures.why: Works as both jazz drummer and electronic producer, which is exactly the scene's premise.

keyFigures.name: Theon Cross
keyFigures.why: Made the tuba a lead bass instrument capable of sub-bass weight and dancehall articulation.

keyFigures.name: Gary Crosby
keyFigures.why: Co-founded Tomorrow's Warriors in 1991; the scene's existence is substantially attributable to that programme.

keyFigures.name: Ezra Collective
keyFigures.why: Won the Mercury Prize in 2023, the first jazz act to do so, playing Afrobeat and reggae-driven jazz.

genres.contested: Whether 'revival' is the right word, since British jazz did not stop — the Jazz Warriors in the 1980s, Courtney Pine, and a continuous free improvisation scene were all active. Critics also note the media framing conflated a genuinely diverse set of bands into one marketable story. Several of the musicians have said they do not consider themselves a scene.

lineage.explanation: Rags were standard New Orleans band repertoire, and the multi-strain march form came across intact — a lot of early jazz is a rag played by a band. What changed is that the printed notes stopped being binding: players began paraphrasing the strains, and blues inflection entered a music that had none. Jelly Roll Morton's Red Hot Peppers sides are rag architecture with improvisation and blues poured into it.

Stride is ragtime's alternating bass with the metronome removed. The left-hand mechanism is inherited almost unchanged; what the Harlem players added was swung eighth notes, blues harmony, right-hand improvisation, and a competitive tempo escalation that had no place in Joplin's instruction to never play fast.

Young Chicagoans learned the New Orleans front line off King Oliver and Armstrong records and then reweighted it. The collective texture thinned, the saxophone pushed in, tempos rose, and the individual solo chorus began displacing the group weave — the change that makes the swing small group possible.

The big band took the New Orleans front line's division of labour and multiplied it into sections: what one clarinet did against one cornet, five reeds now do against four trumpets. Fletcher Henderson's charts are the translation step, turning improvised counterpoint into written call-and-response.

Armstrong established that a jazz singer phrases like a horn player — displacing the beat, bending pitch, treating the written melody as a suggestion — and popularised scat as an extension of that. Every jazz singer after him is working from this premise whether or not they scat.

The territory bands working the Midwest carried the New Orleans repertoire and instrumentation outward, but the KC scene reweighted it toward blues form and riff construction, which the New Orleans model used far less.

Ellington learned directly from Willie 'The Lion' Smith and James P. Johnson, and the harmonic richness of his orchestral writing comes out of stride's keyboard voicings scaled up to a horn section. The stride left hand is also what the swing rhythm section replaced — the bass and guitar took over the job one hand had been doing.

Chicago's shift from a two-beat march feel toward an even four, and its promotion of the individual solo over collective improvisation, are the two things swing then standardised. Gene Krupa carried the Chicago drive straight into Benny Goodman's band.

The Basie rhythm section arrived in New York in 1936 and changed the era's feel from underneath: even four-to-the-bar, timekeeping moved to the hi-hat and ride, bass drum reserved for accents, and enormous space. Every swing band adjusted. Riff-based head arrangements spread the same way.

The big band vocalist slot gave singers a professional route and fixed the repertoire as the popular songbook. Holiday's small-group sides for Teddy Wilson are the version where the singer is a soloist among soloists rather than a feature act.

Django and Grappelli took the American swing repertoire and its harmony wholesale, then rebuilt the rhythm section without drums, piano or horns. The other parent is not on this map: Romani string-band practice and Parisian musette, which supply the ornamentation, the minor-key chromaticism and the fingered vibrato.

Bebop kept swing's harmony and rhythmic base and rejected almost everything else: the big band, the written arrangement, the dance floor, the entertainment function, and the economics that put Black musicians in front of white audiences as employees. The small group playing at tempos nobody could dance to was a position, not just a sound.

Charlie Parker came out of Jay McShann's Kansas City band, and Lester Young's light tone, long asymmetric phrases and behind-the-beat placement are the direct model for bebop line construction. The KC jam-session culture — many choruses, blues form, cutting contests — is bebop's working method before bebop existed.

Bud Powell's right hand is Parker's line and his left hand is stride's, stripped to sparse rootless punctuation. The route runs through Art Tatum, whose substitutions and passing harmony gave the bebop generation most of its reharmonisation vocabulary.

Sarah Vaughan and Eddie Jefferson brought bebop harmony and phrasing into singing, and vocalese — writing lyrics to a recorded improvised solo and singing it — makes the debt literal. Vaughan sang with Earl Hines and Billy Eckstine's bands alongside Parker and Gillespie.

Machito's Afro-Cubans, with Mario Bauzá as musical director, put a full jazz horn section and big-band arranging over a Cuban rhythm section. The orchestration is American; the rhythmic organisation underneath is entirely Cuban, and the two do not blend so much as coexist under tension.

Gillespie hired Chano Pozo in 1947 and 'Manteca' and 'Cubana Be, Cubana Bop' followed within months. Bebop supplied the harmonic language and the soloing; Pozo supplied clave, the tumbao and drum patterns carried from Afro-Cuban religious practice. The swing lilt is what got discarded — the eighth notes go straight.

The Miles Davis nonet kept bebop's harmony and threw out its heat: soft attack, no vibrato, medium tempos, and written contrapuntal arrangement where bebop had head-and-blow. Gil Evans' charts restore the arranger to the centre of a music that had just deposed him.

Lester Young's dry, vibratoless tenor and unhurried melodic placement is what 'cool' names as a sound. Lee Konitz and Stan Getz descend from Young rather than from Parker, which is why they are the two major post-war saxophonists who do not sound like everyone else.

Mulligan and other nonet alumni moved to Los Angeles and found a studio-musician labour pool that could read anything. The piano-less quartet took the nonet's contrapuntal premise and reduced it to two horns implying the harmony between them.

Same quintet, same changes, same head–solos–head. What hard bop adds is weight and blues content: slower tempos, heavier drums, composed introductions and interludes, and heads written to be memorable rather than abstract.

Hard bop's heat is aimed at cool jazz's restraint, and the aim was partly racial and geographic: an East Coast, largely Black music positioning itself against a West Coast, largely white studio scene that the press had been treating as jazz's future. Gospel and rhythm-and-blues content was reclaimed rather than merely added.

The nonet's arrangers — John Lewis, Gunther Schuller, Gil Evans — are the same people who then argued for a formal marriage with concert music. Schuller played French horn on the nonet sessions before he coined 'third stream' at Brandeis in 1957.

The Los Angeles scene's appetite for fugue, canon and unusual instrumentation put it halfway to third stream already. Jimmy Giuffre's drumless chamber groups and Shorty Rogers' woodwind writing sit on the boundary.

Soul jazz is hard bop with the gospel and R&B content promoted from flavour to structure, and the Hammond organ replacing piano and bass. Horace Silver's funky tunes are the shared ancestor both styles claim; the split happens when the backbeat and the vamp stop being devices and become the format.

The riff-over-blues construction and the long open jam are Kansas City procedures reappearing in a neighbourhood bar twenty years later. Interpretation: the organ trio's working economy — nightly, local, audience-facing — is closer to 1930s KC than to the 1950s concert circuit.

Bebop handed a soloist a chord every two beats; modal jazz hands them one scale for sixteen bars. The reduction is aimed squarely at bebop's harmonic congestion — Miles Davis described wanting fewer chords so there was more to do with each one.

Bill Evans brought Ravel- and Debussy-derived voicings into the Davis sextet, and those quartal, ambiguous chords are what make static harmony sound rich rather than empty. Davis himself carried the cool tone and the taste for space directly across.

George Russell's Lydian Chromatic Concept, published in 1953, supplied the theoretical frame that let musicians think in scales rather than chords. Russell taught it to Davis and Evans among others; it is the closest thing modal jazz has to a written source.

The Rio musicians who built bossa nova were listening to Mulligan, Chet Baker and Barney Kessel records — the soft attack, the restraint and the absence of vibrato come from there. Jobim's harmony draws on Debussy as much as on jazz, but the performance manner is cool jazz's.

Gilberto's near-inaudible delivery is a deliberate rejection of the big-voiced Brazilian singing of the era, and the model for singing quietly and conversationally into a microphone was American. The songbook idea — a body of harmonically rich standards that instrumentalists then colonise — repeats exactly.

Same Blue Note quintets, same players, often the same session week. What changes is that the forms stop being regular and the harmony stops resolving — Wayne Shorter and Herbie Hancock were writing hard bop dates in 1961 and post-bop ones by 1964.

Post-bop takes modal jazz's harmonic ambiguity and puts it back inside moving forms, so the chords change but never resolve. The Davis quintet's 'time, no changes' approach is modal freedom applied to a rhythm section rather than to a scale.

Post-bop is what musicians made after hearing Ornette Coleman and deciding to go partway. Tony Williams' elastic time, Andrew Hill's asymmetric forms and the habit of playing deliberately outside the harmony all depend on free jazz having made those moves thinkable first.

Ornette Coleman came up playing rhythm-and-blues and bebop in Texas and Los Angeles, and the quartet that arrived at the Five Spot in 1959 kept hard bop's melodic directness while removing the chord sequence entirely. The hostility from hard bop musicians was immediate and personal.

Modal jazz had already reduced harmonic motion to almost nothing; free jazz took the last step and removed the pre-agreed frame altogether. Coltrane's route runs directly through this — the extended vamps of 'Impressions' become the open playing of 1965 without an obvious break.

Cecil Taylor studied at the New England Conservatory and his atonal cluster language owes more to Bartók, Stockhausen and Henry Cowell than to any jazz pianist. The permission to abandon tonality came partly from European concert music, which third stream had already brought into the room.

Interpretation, though one participants made themselves: collective simultaneous improvisation with no designated soloist is a New Orleans procedure returning after forty years of one-at-a-time soloing. Ornette Coleman's Free Jazz double quartet and Albert Ayler's use of marches and hymns both make the connection audible rather than merely arguable.

The AACM's founding generation were playing free jazz in Chicago before the organisation existed. What the collective added was structure — composed sections, notated frames, and a refusal of the continuous-blowing model that New York had made standard.

Anthony Braxton's compositional apparatus, Muhal Richard Abrams' orchestral writing and Roscoe Mitchell's use of silence all draw on twentieth-century concert music as directly as third stream did — but from inside a Black self-organised institution rather than through the conservatory. That difference is the point.

'Great Black Music, Ancient to the Future' is a claim on the whole history, and the Art Ensemble made it audible by putting marches, field hollers and New Orleans polyphony inside free improvisation. The vocalised brass timbres and the collective front line are reached for deliberately, not inherited passively.

A Love Supreme is a modal record with a devotional programme attached: a bass ostinato functioning as a drone, one mode held for minutes, and a chanted mantra where a head would be. Everything the idiom does harmonically is already in the modal toolkit.

Overblowing, multiphonics and collective ecstatic climaxes come straight from the free jazz vocabulary — Pharoah Sanders was in Coltrane's late band and Sun Ra's before that. The difference is intent: the same sounds are framed as devotion rather than as rupture.

European improvisers took free jazz's central permission and then rejected the rest of it as American idiom: the blues inflection, the residual pulse, the saxophone-as-preaching-voice, the whole gestural vocabulary. Derek Bailey's term 'non-idiomatic' is aimed at free jazz as much as at bebop, and the politics of refusing American cultural dominance were stated openly.

The Art Ensemble and other AACM members moved to Paris in 1969 and recorded prolifically for BYG Actuel, putting little instruments, extreme dynamic contrast and composed framing in front of European improvisers who were already working in that direction. Traffic ran both ways from then on.

Interpretation: Jimmy Giuffre's 1961–62 trio with Paul Bley and Steve Swallow — no drums, near-silent dynamics, free but chamber-scaled — anticipates the quiet end of European improvisation by several years. The direct historical link is thin; the resemblance is not.

Same music, different economics. When the club circuit closed to free players, they rented lofts and became their own promoters — which removed set lengths, drink minimums and owner veto, and produced longer, more patient performances than any club would have allowed.

The AACM and St. Louis's BAG both sent members to New York in the early 1970s, and they brought the self-organising model and the compositional discipline with them. The all-saxophone ensemble and the duo format both flourish here for the same reason: they are cheap and they demand structure.

Fusion's harmony is modal jazz's — one chord for a long time — transferred to a Fender Rhodes and set over a rock backbeat. The two parents not on this map are rock and funk, which supply the volume, the straight eighths and the electric instruments.

The personnel are identical: Hancock, Shorter, Williams, Corea, Zawinul and Holland all came out of the post-bop world and went electric more or less at once. The interactive rhythm-section thinking of the Davis quintet survives the change of instruments.

Soul jazz had been amplifying jazz for over a decade — the Hammond organ, the electric guitar, the R&B backbeat — and had absorbed the critical contempt for it first. Fusion's electric turn is less unprecedented than the 1970s controversy suggested.

Airto Moreira played on Bitches Brew and then with Weather Report and Return to Forever, and Flora Purim sang on the latter. Brazilian percussion and straight-eighth feels are woven into fusion from the beginning rather than added later.

The organ trio's groove-first premise scaled up: horn sections, clavinet, electric bass, and a sixteenth-note funk feel replacing the shuffle. The soloist's role shrinks further, and the bass line becomes the composition.
